chapters.summary: Council staff opens the hearing, asks attendees to silence devices and not approach the dais, and directs anyone wanting to testify to see the sergeant-at-arms. Staff then tells Chair Stevens the committee is ready to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives procedural instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Children and Youth.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, we ask that you please silence all electronic devices and at no time, at no time are you to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you have any questions or would like to sign up for in-person testimony, please see one of the sergeant-at-arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair Stevens, we're ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Althea Stevens welcomes everyone and thanks them for dealing with a location change due to high turnout. She says the topic is very important and thanks attendees for staying through the process.
chapters.title: Chair Stevens welcomes attendees and explains hearing location change

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you all for dealing with us as we change locations.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As you guys can see, there's a lot of people here because this is a very important topic, and we did not all fit in 250.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you for being here, and thank you for staying with us and being through this process.

chapters.summary: Stevens identifies herself as Chair of the Committee on Children and Youth and opens the oversight hearing on secure detention conditions and youth incarceration. She declares that New York City's youth detention systems are in a crisis, citing 352 young people held against about 244 certified beds.
chapters.title: Stevens opens oversight hearing on secure detention crisis

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Councilmember Althea Stevens, Chair of the Committee on Children and Youth.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you all for being here today on our oversight hearing on secure detention conditions and youth incarceration policies in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to be clear why we're here today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: New York City's youth detention systems are in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As of last week, Crossroad and Horizon held a combined population of 352 young people in detention in a detention facility with about with us 244 certification of beds.

chapters.summary: Stevens says the population has climbed every quarter for more than a year. She describes youth sleeping in spaces not meant for sleeping, receiving inadequate education, and staff stretched to the breaking point after her facility tours.
chapters.title: Stevens details overcrowding and unsafe conditions in detention

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is not a temporary surge.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This population has climbed every quarter more.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Every quarter for more than a year.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Young people are sleeping in spaces that were never meant for sleeping, receiving,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: inadequate education and being funneled into a detention system that cannot meet their basic everyday needs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Staff are stretched thin to the breaking point.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Every person in those buildings, young people and staff alike, deserve better than the treatment they are receiving right now.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have toured these facilities several times to see the conditions for myself, and what I see is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We cannot claim to be a city that believes in young people while holding them in conditions like what I've seen.

chapters.summary: Stevens recalls calling for the release of 150 young people from secure detention in September and says the call was a response to an emergency. She cites March 2020, when city agencies, courts, prosecutors, and defenders safely reduced the detention population during COVID-19.
chapters.title: Stevens calls for release of 150 youth and cites COVID-19 precedent

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is why in September I called for the release of 150 young people from secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That call was not radical.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It was a response to an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In March 2020, when COVID-19 threatened the health of everyone

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: inside those facilities, the city, the court, prosecutors, and defenders came together and safely brought the detention population down within weeks.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We know what can be done.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We need a greater urgency.

chapters.summary: Stevens says more than 96% of held youth charged as juvenile or adolescent offenders are Black and Hispanic. She notes long pretrial detentions, with some held more than six months and others more than four years, and youth turning 18 behind walls.
chapters.title: Stevens highlights racial disparities and long pretrial detention

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We also cannot ignore who is being held.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: More than 96% of the young people held in juvenile offenders and adolescent offenders charged are black and Hispanic youth.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The typical young person charged as an adolescent offender has been held for more than six months before their case is resolved, and some have been held for more than four years.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The vast majority of those in secure detention are being held pre-trial.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Many enter as teenagers and turn 18 behind those walls.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Whatever the outcome of those cases, those delays are robbing young people of the time they will never get back.

chapters.summary: Stevens acknowledges the administration's press release plan to improve secure detention and reduce overcrowding. She says the plan lacks funding, timeline, and follow-through details, and the committee wants specific numbers and dates.
chapters.title: Stevens criticizes administration plan for lacking funding and timeline

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Early this year, the Administration of Children's Services, the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice, and the Department of Probation issued a press release about a plan to improve secure detention conditions and reduce overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I welcome any serious efforts to address this crisis, but a plan is only as good as funding and a timeline.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: and its follow through.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And the press release failed to include any of those critical details.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Today, this committee intends to investigate exactly what steps this administration plans to take, including how they will be funded, how things will be funded, and when New Yorkers can expect to see real results.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We want specific numbers, dates, not general commitments.

chapters.summary: Stevens says existing alternative-to-detention and reentry programs are underfunded and underutilized. She argues the city does not need to reinvent the wheel but should capitalize on existing resources.
chapters.title: Stevens says existing alternatives should be funded and used

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We know that there are exiting programs that provide us to alternative detention and incarceration, as well as a transitional program that is designed to ease the reentry process for young people post-release.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In this case,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It is not about reinventing the wheel to find solutions, but capitalizing upon existing resources that are underfunded and underutilized.

chapters.summary: Stevens introduces Intro 447, which she sponsors, requiring ACS and partner agencies to develop a guide on alternatives to incarceration and detention. The guide would be distributed to judges, attorneys, public defenders, youth advocates, and district attorneys.
chapters.title: Stevens introduces Intro 447 on alternatives guide

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In addition to the oversight topics, we will also hear four pieces of legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Introduction 447, which I'm proud to sponsor, will require ACS and

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: in consultation with DYC, DYCD, DOP, and O and Mach J to develop a guide of information about alternatives to incarcerations and alternatives to

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: detention for distribution to judges, attorneys, public defenders, and youth advocates and district attorneys.

chapters.summary: Stevens introduces Intro 629, sponsored by Councilmember Restler, requiring ACS to establish teams to review every young person held in secure detention. The teams would recommend candidates for early release or early case resolution.
chapters.title: Stevens introduces Intro 629 on youth detention review teams

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Introduction 629 sponsored by

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Councilmember Rester would require ACS to establish terms to review the circumstances of every young person held in secure detention and recommend candidates for early release.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: or early case resolution.

chapters.summary: Stevens introduces Intro 977, sponsored by Councilmember Lewis, requiring ACS and DYCD to provide annual training on identifying sexually exploited youth. She also introduces Reso 274, which calls for New York City to participate in Raise the Age program funding.
chapters.title: Stevens introduces Intro 977 and Reso 274

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Introduction 977 sponsored by Councilmember Lewis will require ACS and DYCD to

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: provide annual trainings to staff on identifying sexually exploited youth, including risk factors, common indicators, and trauma-informed resources and available support services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Reso 274, which I'm also sponsoring, calls for the

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: enactment of legislation that will require, would entitle New York City to participate in New York City State's Raise the Age program funding.

chapters.summary: Stevens tells agencies to explain what is working, what is not, and what resources are needed. She thanks committee staff and her district team, and asks whether Farrah is present.
chapters.title: Stevens tells agencies what committee needs and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the agencies testifying today, we need you to know that what is working, what is not, and what resources and administrations needed to address these issues.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the young people in our care and family, in their families, we see you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We are not going to stop pushing until these conditions change.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I would like to thank my committee staff, senior policy analyst Elizabeth Arts, senior committee counsel Ray O.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Rie Rosswell.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yep, look at me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: To their hard work in preparing for this hearing and to the team back in the district, Suite 16 and Greer-Mainhew.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is Farrah here?

chapters.summary: Stevens reads a statement from Councilmember Lewis on Intro 977. Lewis says sexual exploitation and trafficking are devastating, and staff who work with youth must be trained to recognize warning signs and provide trauma-informed care and connections to services.
chapters.title: Stevens reads Councilmember Lewis statement on Intro 977

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Now we'll read a brief statement from Councilmember Lewis on her bill.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Althea Stevens, that's me, for her leadership.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: For her leadership on the Committee on Children and Youth and for her commitment to protecting the safety and well-being of young people across our city, I'm proud to sponsor Intro 977, which will require the administration of Children's Services and Department of Youth

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: of Community Development to provide an annual training for staff who work directly with young people on identifying sexually exploited young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sexual exploitation and trafficking have been a devastating consequence, and young people experiencing exploitation may face significant barriers in seeking help.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The adults who work with those

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: them must be equipped to recognize warning signs, understand risk factors, respond with trauma, inform care, and connect young people to available support services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This legislation ensures that staff receive consistent training to better identify vulnerable young youth and respond with the knowledge and sensitivity those young people deserve.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Every young person deserves to be safe, support, and protected from exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: By strengthening training and awareness, we can help ensure that young people are recognized, believed, connected to the resources they need that

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That concludes Councilmember Lewis's remarks.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I will turn it over to Councilmember Ressler to give his opening remarks on his legislation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The public advocate, I believe he has opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams thanks Chair Stevens and the committee for holding the hearing. He raises the importance of ensuring eligible youth in custody can vote, citing his Intro 797 requiring DOC reporting on voting at Rikers.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams raises voting rights for youth in custody

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And thank you for always making sure we're focused on our children no matter where they are.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As I mentioned, my name is Jermaine Williams, public advocate for the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Again, I want to thank Chair Stevens and the members of the Committee on Children and Youth for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: First, as Election Day approaches and the city is already engaged in early voting, I want to underscore the importance of ensuring that youth in custody who are eligible to vote are able to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Last week, the City Council passed legislation I sponsored, Intro 797, that requires the Department of Corrections to report on voting activity in Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: All eligible New Yorkers should be able to exercise their right to vote, regardless of whether or not they are incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That should also include ACS and our children in these facilities.

chapters.summary: Williams discusses the Mamdani administration's plan to reduce secure detention and improve conditions. He says the July average daily population at Crossroads and Horizon was 385 despite a 244-person limit, with youth sleeping in boats in hallways and classrooms.
chapters.title: Williams describes overcrowding and sleeping conditions in secure detention

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In September, the Mamdani administration announced a new plan to invest in the city's youth.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This plan aims to reduce the number of young people in secure detention, improve the conditions who are in custody, and strengthen resources in the community.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: While the number of those in secure detention has plummeted from its peak in the super predator days of the 80s and 90s, the city currently does not have enough beds for all of the young people in its custody.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In July, the average daily population at Crossroads and High Horizon was 385 people.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Though they are not supposed to house more than 244 people.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Many youth in secure detention sleep in quote-unquote barker bunks.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: called boats or shallow plastic tubes with a mattress on the floor.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In hallways or spaces like classrooms, disrupting their sleep and education, restricting their access to bathrooms, and adding pressure to an already high-stress environment.

chapters.summary: Williams criticizes inadequate education for youth in secure detention. He says many arrive behind grade level or have disabilities, and many Passage Academy students do not receive required special education plans within 30 days.
chapters.title: Williams criticizes inadequate education and reentry services

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: New York City has long failed to provide an adequate education to youth in secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This population is more likely to arrive behind their grade level and are disproportionately likely to have a learning or emotional disability.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I would say New York City has failed to provide children even outside of these detention facilities adequate education, but that's for a different hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Many of the students enrolled in Passage Academy, which provides education to students in ACS custody, do not receive the special education plan to which they are entitled within 30 days of enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is no surprise then that those released from detention have difficulty reconnecting with or engaging education.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There is a clear need for more transitional services for those exiting detention to help youth and their families ensure that these students re-enroll.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And attend school.

chapters.summary: Williams says violence and contraband remain persistent issues in youth detention centers. He cautions against broad expansion of secure detention beds, saying the focus should be on incarcerating fewer young people.
chapters.title: Williams addresses violence and cautions against expanding beds

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Violence and contraband are also persistent issues at the city's youth detention centers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Jail is a stressful environment for anyone, let alone young people who are still learning to regulate their emotions and settle interpersonal conflicts.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The overcrowding and inconsistent access to structured activities such as schools only exacerbate the existing pressures of being in lockup.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: While every young person in custody must have their own space in which to sleep, and ACS is renovating its detention facilities to accommodate more youth, I just want to caution against any broad expansions in securing detention beds.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Too many times we have seen that if we build it, they will come.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Mayor's plan to improve conditions, attention, increase services and resources in the community is an important step.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And a reminder that we should be focused less on increasing capacity and more on incarcerating fewer young people.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: For too long, we have focused resources on removing people from our communities instead of supporting those communities directly.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Under this new administration, we have a chance to make meaningful, lasting change for young people in the city.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know this is a difficult conversation for everyone involved.

chapters.summary: Williams recognizes Anthony Wells, president of Local 371, and other unions present. He says staff need resources and hopes everyone can work together so young people return to their communities in better condition.
chapters.title: Williams thanks union Local 371 and calls for collaboration

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to recognize that there haven't been Anthony Wells, president of Local 371, and a lot of the unions who are here.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know you're doing as best job as you can there, and you know you need resources as well, so hopefully we can work together to figure this out so everybody feels safe and is safe, and young people return to the communities hopefully in a better condition than they came in.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens thanks Public Advocate Williams and notes the expanded committee attendance. She acknowledges Councilmembers Felder, Joseph, Williams, Nurse, Ossé, Hanif, and Restler, then calls the first panel.
chapters.title: Stevens thanks Public Advocate and recognizes expanded committee

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, Public Advocate, for being here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And as you guys can see, we also have an expanded committee today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So shout out to all my colleagues who are here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you, Councilmember Felder, Joseph, Williams, Nurse, Osei, Hanif, and Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you guys all for being here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: He said he didn't want to open it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Oh, oh, you didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, well, Lincoln would like to do it.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Lincoln Restler thanks Chair Stevens for arranging council tours of Horizon and Crossroads. He says the secure detention population more than doubled from about 140 under Eric Adams to approximately 360, and criticizes cuts to prevention and ATI programs.
chapters.title: Restler thanks Chair Stevens for tours and warns population doubled

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to take a moment to thank the chair who

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: you know, everybody says is like the biggest and best fighter for our young people, which is true.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But she did something special in advance of this hearing, which is that she invited many of us in the council to come on tours of Horizons and Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So almost everybody who's up here today

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: over the last four or five weeks has spent time in Horizons, in Crossroads, and seen for ourselves just how troubling the situation is.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I really want to thank you for your leadership on this issue because it is an urgent one.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, when the population of children in secure detention, the population of children in secure detention has more than doubled over the past five years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It was just about 140 when Eric Adams came into office.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Today, I don't know, we'll get the testimony from ACS, but we're approximately at 360.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Instead of investing in preventative programs,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: like Next Steps and ATI programs that were eliminated, Eric Adams and his team chose to cut these programs and build more and more beds for kids in jail.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is the wrong approach.

chapters.summary: Restler points to the Rikers population review team as a model and says Intro 629 would create youth population review teams. He acknowledges concerns about confidentiality and ACS's role, and says he looks forward to amending the bill.
chapters.title: Restler advocates youth population review teams and Intro 629

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: At Rikers, we implemented a successful population review team approach where city agencies, attorneys, nonprofit leaders, and the courts all come together to review cases and determine what's needed to secure someone's release from jail.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It could be helping secure the right housing placement or finding the right ATI program or mental health provider, the missing piece that allows the courts to release an individual into the community prior to trial.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We need to take this same approach for our youth.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There is urgency.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 629 would require the creation of youth population review teams.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Every single case should be carefully analyzed to see if an individual can be released and supported in the community while their case proceeds.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I understand that there are some very real concerns with the current draft of the legislation about confidentiality and the role of ACS and the best way to structure these teams.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I look forward to working with the administration and advocates and, of course, Chair Stevens to make the necessary changes.

chapters.summary: Restler supports Chair Stevens' legislation to create a comprehensive ATI and ATD guide. He says the Mamdani plan is a step, but the city must center decarceration and drive the population back to pre-Adams levels.
chapters.title: Restler supports ATI guide and urges decarceration

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I also strongly support Chair Stevens'legislation to develop a comprehensive plan, a comprehensive guide of all ATI and ATD programs so that we can make sure public defenders and judges are aware of every possible program

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: that might be a good fit for a child.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like our public advocate said, I'm great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: that Mayor Mumdani and his team announced a plan for how we're going to be able to better care for the young people who are in custody, in detention today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There should not be kids sleeping in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we need to center decarceration and reducing

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: urgently reducing the unnecessary incarceration of our young people and driving that number down back to the pre-Eric Adams total.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We can do it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've done it before.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's going to take a whole-of-government approach.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's going to need to be a priority like it hasn't been before.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And with Chair Stevens leading the way, I'm hopeful that we can get there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.text: At this time, I will be calling our first panel, which will be D.A.

chapters.summary: Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark thanks the committee and begins with Bronx youth violence statistics. She says the Bronx has about 20% of the city's youth but a disproportionate share of youth gun arrests, shooting victims, and shooting defendants.
chapters.title: Bronx DA Darcel Clark opens with Bronx youth violence statistics

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Stevens and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you so much for giving me this opportunity to speak with you today to testify on secure detention conditions and youth incarceration policies in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The Bronx is home to about 20% of New York City residents younger than 18 years old, yet it accounts for a disproportionate share of youth gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: About a third of youth gun arrests and youth shooting victims and nearly half of youth shooting defendants are in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: These figures underscore the urgency of our responsibility to protect young people, support victims, and keep our communities safe.

chapters.summary: Clark says she will focus on youth justice operations, information-sharing challenges, and investment in interventions. She describes Raise the Age and her office's Youth Justice Bureau, which began accepting cases in July 2025 and considers mental health, family history, education, and intervention options.
chapters.title: Clark outlines focus areas and Raise the Age Youth Justice Bureau

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Today, I will focus on three areas that warrant the Council's attention.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: How our youth justice system operates, the information sharing challenges that affect detention safety

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: and case decision making, along with the need for sustained investment in effective youth interventions.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: In 2017, New York's Raise the Age law established a framework for 13 to 17 year olds

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: charged with serious felony offenses, intending to balance accountability with opportunities for rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: To strengthen this work, my office established a Youth Justice Bureau, and with me today is the Chief of the Youth Justice Bureau, Marcel Edouard, and Deputy Chief of the Bureau, Ginger James.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So we established that in March of 2025 and the Bureau began accepting cases this past July.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Before that, the cases were scattered throughout my office, so now I have a concentrated place where those cases are happening.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Assistant District Attorneys with Youth

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The Assistant District Attorneys with the Youth Justice Bureau consider mental health, substance use, family history, education, employment, and intervention options when reviewing these cases.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Depending on the facts and circumstances of each case, recommendations can range from a conditional discharge and probation to incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Our objective is to make informed, individualized decisions that recognize the seriousness of the offense while considering the best available path to accountability and reducing future harm.

chapters.summary: Clark says prosecutors cannot fully assess youth needs when information is fragmented across systems. She says her office has struggled to get daily updates on Bronx youth detained at Horizon and Crossroads, and cites the June violent uprising at Horizon as a safety concern.
chapters.title: Clark says fragmented information and ACS data gaps hinder decisions

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Prosecutors cannot fully assess a young person's needs, risks, or appropriate interventions.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: when critical information remains fragmented across the system.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Legal restrictions and agency-specific policies can limit access to details about a young person's prior involvement with the justice system,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: including cases handled in family court or through services provided by the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: These challenges are particularly significant when young people are in secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: My office has experienced difficulty obtaining daily updates identifying Bronx youth involved in Bronx cases who are detained at Horizon and Crossroads Juvenile Detention Centers.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The Administration for Children's Services maintains the most current information about the young people in its custody.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Yet, despite our requests, we have not received the daily detention population information needed to compile an accurate, up-to-date count of Bronx youth in these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: This is not simply an administrative gap, but a major safety risk as well.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The need for coordination was accented by the violent uprising at Horizon in June,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: when detained youth and staff members were slashed and beaten, and ACS reportedly struggled to maintain control of the facility for several hours.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The situation raised serious concerns about the safety of the

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: of young people in city custody and the staff responsible for their care.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: My office is prosecuting certain individuals for additional charges arising from that incident, which highlights another area of concern.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: At times, my office has struggled to obtain information about alleged infractions, violations, and other conduct by youth in detention that may signal a safety risk or give rise to additional criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We must protect the confidentiality rights of young people while improving coordination among the agencies responsible for prosecution,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: supervision, services, and detention so that officials have the information necessary to make sound decisions and respond to safety threats.

chapters.summary: Clark says New York City counties are excluded from Raise the Age reimbursement because of property tax cap and local plan requirements. She describes her office's gun diversion programs, JIBI pilot for high-needs youth, and Bronx Restore with BRAG and Bronx Connect.
chapters.title: Clark describes Raise the Age exclusion and Bronx diversion programs

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Beyond the changes to how young people are prosecuted, Raise the Age also

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: was designed to offer funding for programs and services that address the root causes of youth violence and turn young offenders away from negative behavior.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: However, that investment remains a significant concern for New York City's five counties, which have been excluded from the state's existing reimbursement structure

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: because of eligibility requirements tied to the property tax cap and local implementation plans.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: My office has not allowed those funding challenges to delay our pursuit of appropriate programs and services.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We have acquired grants and committed resources to develop initiatives that aim to quell violence, promote rehabilitation, and expand opportunities for young people.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: First, our gun diversion programs, operated in partnership with the Osborne Association and the Fortune Society, serve eligible 16

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: and all the way up to 39-year-olds charged with gun possession who have no prior felony convictions.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: They plead guilty to a felony, receive intensive services for a year, including therapy, counseling, help with school or work, and mentorship with regular check-ins before a judge.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: If they complete the program successfully and not re-arrested within 90 days of completion, their pleas can be vacated and charges dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Second, Justice Innovation for Bronx Youth, or JIBI as we call it, is a pilot initiative providing holistic programming to vulnerable youth.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: These are young adults charged with serious or violent offenses, and many existing youth programs will not accept them for services.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Participants are connected to mental health and

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: substance use professionals, credible messenger services, and spiritual guidance and life coach mentors to help turn their lives around.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Third, Bronx Restore is a pilot prevention program being developed by BRAG, which is one of our Cure Violence Group, Bronx Rises Against Guns, and Bronx Connect.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It is designed to serve 30 teens and young adults in the St.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Mary's area of the 40th precinct and Fordham section of the 46th precinct.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Participants will have access to mentorship, internships, life skills training, and case management throughout the year-long program.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: They will also be paid $25 an hour for their participation, allowing them to not only invest in themselves, but in their financial futures as well.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: These programs reflect our commitment to prevention and intervention alongside prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But we must also assess whether they reach the young people who need them, whether participants complete them, and whether the services provide measurable improvements in safety and long-term outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Sustained funding, coordination among agencies, and meaningful evaluation are essential to that.

chapters.summary: Clark urges the council to examine whether agencies share timely information, whether safety incidents and misconduct are documented, whether detained youth access services, and whether investments produce results. She says accountability and safety are not mutually exclusive.
chapters.title: Clark urges council to examine information sharing and results

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I urge the council to examine whether agencies share appropriate, timely information about Bronx youth in custody, whether significant safety incidents and alleged misconduct are documented and communicated effectively,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: whether detained young people have access to appropriate services and intervention,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: and whether public investments in youth justice are producing measurable results.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We must hold young people accountable for serious conduct while ensuring that they are safe within our care while reducing the likelihood of future harm.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: These goals are not mutually exclusive.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: They require reliable information, clear lines of responsibility, effective services, and measurable results.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I welcome continued collaboration with the City Council and other stakeholders to strengthen these events to promote safer outcomes for young people and communities throughout New York City, especially the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you very much for allowing me to present.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And I'll take any questions if you have any.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether the JIBI and Bronx Restore pilot programs are funded by the DA's office. Clark says the office applies for grants and provides matching funds, and describes JIBI as a small pilot aimed at youth other programs reject.
chapters.title: Stevens questions DA Clark on pilot funding and duration

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm D.A.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Clark.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We really appreciate you being here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And you have always been very loud and vocal about wanting to make sure that young people don't even reach you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so not only have you been talking about preventative stuff, but I just have some questions about some of these pilot programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You spoke about like the Justice Innovation for the Bronx, the JIB, and the Bronx Restore.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Are those all programs that the DA's office is funding?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, some of it, we have grants.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We receive grants to get the money, but none of it was, it's my office and the grants that we have.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the grants that you guys have seeked to get to run these other programs.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We apply for the grants in order to do these programs because we found that there were not enough programming to address these particular issues.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I put up funding as well, so we match what they give us.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How long have these pilots have been going?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, when did they start?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How long is the time period for these pilots?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Do you want to know that?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, we just started.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The Jibby was awarded, I believe, two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So we're still in the process of putting it together, having the stakeholders, identifying the youth.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's a small pilot.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We have to see if it worked first.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We never jump right in without knowing for sure whether or not it's going to work.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's helpful because these are young people that other programs that even exist now will not take.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But meanwhile, I have them, and I want to do something for them.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't want to see them in Horizons or Crossroads if I don't have to.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So if there are alternatives to the detention, this is one of them that we're looking to use.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, one of the things that one of my colleagues when we were on the visit was asking was just around some of the programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you have certain qualities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: around some mental health issues or an IEP, it disqualifies you from some of the programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm happy to hear that you guys are stepping up and creating programs that can reach some of those kids that some of these other programs aren't accepting.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I would love to continue to hear about the progress and see how these policies are going, because if they're working, then how do we then as a city continue to adopt those and make that standard?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about Clark's testimony that her office does not receive daily detention updates. Clark says she receives daily Rikers lists but not Horizon or Crossroads lists, making it hard to assess who is inside and who might be released to alternatives.
chapters.title: Stevens asks Clark about missing daily detention updates

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions because I have some colleagues who have some questions as well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: One of the things you mentioned in your testimony was around the daily updates of the detention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Could you talk a little bit about that and why aren't you getting these daily updates and what that actually can do for your office and why you would want that?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: All right, so if we're talking about reducing the population, which we need to do because we all know that there's overcrowding, right?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't want any of the kids in there if we don't have to.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But when you look at the charges that they're charging and the conduct, some people are going to be there, right?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But not everybody should.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And if there's ways that we can deal with them on the outside, you know, we should be able.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: In order for me to be able to evaluate who is inside, I need to know who is inside.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Because when the arrest first happened and the judge may set bail or we get to retain them because they're in the youth part, we know it that day.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Until the next court day, we don't know if they made it out because they made bail or et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So if we had a daily list, we get it for Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I know who's in Rikers every single day.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And as I work with defenders and everyone else, if they want me to look at a particular

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The defendant or you want the city wants me to prioritize those long stayers or those who are in custody.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I need to know who they are.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We don't get that as from horizons or crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I can't answer why.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Just telling you that I don't.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But if I had it, it would be more helpful for us to be able to evaluate who those young people are, what their needs are, whether or not there is an alternative to the detention that they're in now in order for us to assess them.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But without knowing who's there every day, I can't do it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's really helpful because I know, so I just want to also point out, we did meet with all the DAs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I believe we're still trying to meet with Brooklyn, but everyone was like, Darcelle Clark is going to be there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: She got it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Our sister's speaking for us.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They all said that you're speaking on behalf of all of them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Oh, God.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I can tell you about the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I can't tell you what's happening in every other borough, but I can tell you the Bronx.

chapters.summary: Stevens notes other district attorneys defer to Clark and asks why the Bronx has more detained youth. Clark says Bronx crimes and Horizon incidents require attention, and Marcel Edouard explains that one-third of cases are retained in youth part while two-thirds go to family court.
chapters.title: Stevens and Clark discuss Bronx caseload and information needs

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They said, don't worry, Darcelle got it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, because it was also just interesting from those conversations that we had.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, prime example, I think when we were talking to Staten Island, they were like, we only have 12 kids.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We kind of know because it's so small.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And even in Manhattan, I think they said they had about 24 kids, and their youth department is so small, they know because they see them on a regular basis, so it looks different.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, especially for the Bronx specifically, can you talk about, like, why is it so important?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is it that we just have so many more kids, or can I just get a little bit more information on, like, why?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I could give you the stats, but I'm telling you that we account for the number of the kids that are in detention.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The crimes are happening in the Bronx, you know, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And additional crimes or offenses may be happening in the detention center.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: At least I could speak for Horizon because that's under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: which would add on to other charges as well.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So it's important for me to know because I have a lot.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We have a lot of kids that we need to service, a lot of kids that if they were preventive measures, if we could have dealt with the root causes of their crimes before they ended up before me,

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We could deal with that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So that's why we work with the stakeholders, community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I'm doing all I can on the preventive side as well as the prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I'm unapologetic about having to do the prosecution work because if you know who the victims are and the safety conditions for our communities, it's necessary for prosecution to happen, but not everybody needs to be in.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And if we can do something to stabilize them, to turn them around, to let them appreciate, hold them accountable, at least making sure that the public is safe, we'd be better off.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: You want to add?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Yeah, and if I may add something.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: You must remember that it's only one-third, one-third of those coming through the Bronx system that we are retaining in the youth parts.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Two-thirds of them are going to family court.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: So that means that we're assessing those cases early.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We're determining whether those cases should stay in the youth part or not.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And for the most part, we are sending those cases to be treated in family court and receive programs at that level.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But at our level, we're also looking at the one-third that we do retain, and those are the most important.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: much more serious cases that we retain and to see what it is that we can do about providing them with community-based programming as well, which, as you know, did not exist in a large format before.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: At this time, I'm going to turn it over to the public advocate who has a few questions.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Williams says he was surprised Clark is not getting information and asks whether this stems from recent laws. Clark says laws restrict access to school, family, and mental health information, and Ginger James explains Family Court Act and Social Services Law barriers predate Raise the Age.
chapters.title: Williams questions Clark on missing information and Raise the Age

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And thank you, Madam DA.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I've heard you speak about wanting to prevent kids to come in in the first place as well, so I appreciate the work they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Just a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I was surprised to hear you're not getting info.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So is the info that you've asked for before from the, I guess, from ACS or who's?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It sounded like you said you weren't getting info that you needed.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, you mean, I mean, well, as far as the numbers of who's detained, yes, we haven't been able to get that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But there are other things because the law restricts us from knowing certain information that would be helpful to me in order to determine what should we do with a particular child.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's not a one-size-fits-all.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I need to know what this kid's school life was like, if there is even one.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is this from recently passed laws?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: No, this is raise the age.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, raise the age, and even before that, I mean, the laws for youth are very specific, and rightfully so, because we have to have confidentiality about our kids.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But once we talk about developing a raise the age, and you really need me to look at how to, you know, handle them, and whether or not they go to family.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Court or they stay in the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: This information I need to know in order to determine what's the best thing for this child.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So there's information before, there's information you think you needed before raised age.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And raise the age added on to that?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Or was this always the case?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's information you thought you needed that you weren't getting.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, I think it's more so now because more things go to family court.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: There's a presumption to family court now.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So before those kids were before me, 16 years old, they were adults, and I had to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I had to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But now...

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: What information is it you're saying you're not getting?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Their school, you know, the school, you know, what school they go to, the family makeup, their mental health, all kinds of things that we can get from defense attorneys, from outside agencies.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We're not allowed to know that, and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But if you want me to help a kid, you need to give me the information.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I'm not going to use it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I think the fear is that prosecutors are going to use this information to punish the kids.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And that's exactly the opposite of what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But just so I'm clear, the raise the Asian change information you're getting, you're saying just more people are not coming to you, so you can't get that information now.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: What I would say is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: First, you know, we have provisions in the Family Court Act that prevent the family court, the law department, from sharing certain information with us.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That's not raise the age.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: That's pre-raise the age.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: Same thing with social services law, for instance, right?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: So ACS, certain records they can't turn over because of social services law.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: I think the issue is if you want a society where we protect children and we look at what is driving the behavior and how do we address it and how do we set them up for even if they do have to be in detention, how do we set them up for the future?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: You need to know what the needs are so you can match the needs to the proper services.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: And if you don't know what the needs are and we operate in silos, we're not going to make any progress in getting to this generation to stop shooting each other and killing each other, right?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: As to raise the age, I'm sorry, I do want to answer your question, so I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: But as to raise the age itself, what happens is a lot of stuff with the case law that comes out.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: So when we have to respond to certain motions, we do need a sense of, is this youth amenable to services?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: Has the youth received services before?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: What was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: There's a lot of information that could be gleaned that would help us make the determination whether we should send the case to family court for rehabilitative services or whether the case is best stayed with us but still potentially getting rehabilitative services.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The way it came across was like it was a new problem.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I was trying to figure out what the new problem was.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: It's an age-old problem, but it's also, it's becoming a newer problem as we deal with raise the age and how it's shaped up through the case law over the last nine years since its inception.

chapters.summary: Williams praises Brooklyn's Project Restore and asks how the Bronx version is going. Clark says the Bronx got $3 million from the governor, is building the program with BRAG and Bronx Connect, and expects to start next year; she also says she cannot draw a clear link between arrests or lockups and community safety.
chapters.title: Williams asks about Bronx Project Restore and arrests-safety link

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Because I just get worried.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I heard everything blamed on bail, and now I'm hearing everything blamed on raise the age.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: You never hear me in that discussion.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I'm good with that.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Also, I know that the Brooklyn DA is not here, but his project Restore has been phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's been, like, really phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It started in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So now, and I raised hell until I got it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So now I got it.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So, yeah, it's historic.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm not sure, like, everyone should be trying to figure out how to expand this and see if it's expandable.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Like, Brooklyn's had...

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I mean, if you're a victim of crime, that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But the numbers show it's been great.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I just wanted to see how that program was going.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, we just now got it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We got $3 million from the governor.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So that's how we're funding that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And, you know, we have to build it up.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So we identified the community-based organizations that's going to administer it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So it's going to be BRAG and Bronx Connect.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We have an academic component that's going to evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So we're building it up now.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We look to start it in the beginning of the year.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We should be ready to roll it out for the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And lastly, have you seen in your time here a link between how many people we arrest and the safety of Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Residents.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Have you seen a link between how many people you can arrest, how many young people you can arrest and house, and people being safer in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So you're saying if there are more young people arrested, whether or not the Bronx is safer?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't know if we can necessarily say that because an arrest doesn't mean that somebody's going to be detained.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Somebody having charges doesn't mean that they are going to recidivate or not.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I don't know if that's apples to apples comparison.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I deal with what I have.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The arrests that are happening have increased.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they have increased, and I have to accept that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But what we do with each case is different.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So just because somebody is arrested doesn't mean that, you know, one, that they're guilty, first of all.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I've got to prove that beyond a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We don't get this.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So an arrest is one thing.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Getting a case through the process.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I guess the question is, is there also a connection between how many people are, how many young people are locked up and how many people are safe?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I was a resident in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I mean, I would have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't know if they, I don't have that correlation of because so many people are arrested, the community is safer.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I mean, we, look, we deal with mass, we've dealt with mass incarceration for as long, I mean, I've been in this business 40 years now.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I started out when it was nail them in jail and everybody was in jail for the littlest thing.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Was our community safer then?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't know necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But if you look at the numbers now, when I start in 1990, right, we had 2,300 murders in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We got less than 200 right now.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: People are in jail for murder, but it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: You know, it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I can't say that by having somebody in jail makes the community safer.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The communities that have the most resources are the ones that are going to be the safest, not necessarily whether or not somebody's locked up or not.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I don't necessarily see that correlation.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I just want to do all that I can to make sure the community is safe.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And if that means prevention measures, intervention, prosecution, and reentry, all of those things make our community safer.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Not just the rest.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Deputy Speaker.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Amanda Farías asks what factors the DA's office weighs for youth charged with violent felonies. Marcel Edouard describes looking at home, school, prior record, statutory retention prongs, and bail eligibility; Clark says the approach must be holistic and requires more information.
chapters.title: Farías asks factors for detention, release, and ATI for violent felonies

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Hi, DA.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: For young people charged with violent felonies, what factors does your office weigh in deciding whether to seek detention, set non-monetary conditions for release, release under supervision, or offer an ATI program?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: You want to answer that myself?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: What we're going to look at is pretty much everything, and this is why we're here today and why we're talking about cooperation, collaboration, and everyone coming together so that we can

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: have all of the information that we need at the outset when we're dealing with a case to make the right decision.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We would like to, and what we do now with this new bureau, is we look at everything.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We look at every factor.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We look at what is going on with the child at home, what's going on with the child in school, what the circumstances are

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: involved in the particular arrest that we have before us, what this child has done previously if the child has a criminal past.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We look at everything.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: decide whether we're going to retain a case or whether we're going to have that case go to family court or whether we're going to seek bail or whether we're not.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: There are a number of factors that come into play.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: With respect to retention, obviously the law

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: tells you that there are specific things that you have to look for to determine whether a case is going to be retained in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: There are prongs.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: There are legal, if the person displays a weapon, that's one of the prongs.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: That has to exist in order for you to, in furtherance of a crime, for you to retain that case in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: That's something that we look at.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: If the person has done two or three other things that are prongs, we will look at those things and determine whether the person has committed the infraction.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And fits those prongs and keep that case in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But if it doesn't fulfill those requirements that the law required, the prongs that the law required, then that case is going to be considered as a case that we would be sending to family court.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: With respect to bail, if the person

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: you know, has a criminal past, if the person is a person who has shot someone, if the person,

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: you know, has injured someone in a very serious way, obviously we're not trying to have that person go back into the community just like that, okay?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We would like

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: to see what's going on with that person, why that person committed that crime, so we would have to request bail in instances like that.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But it would have to be a bail-eligible offense.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: If it's not a bail-eligible offense, we can't ask for bail.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But if it is, we will ask for bail.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: So there are a number of factors that we look at with respect to bail, not just one thing.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But we need information.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We cannot...

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Proceed with a case if we don't have information, particularly as to the background of that child.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And a lot of times we don't have the information that we need with respect to what that child has committed.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: For instance, if it's in family court case where they had an infraction, we don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We don't have access to that information.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And as a result, you know, there are some decisions that we can't make.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: With respect to what may have occurred previously.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
