utterances.text: And so we move forward and we try to request bail to keep them when the infraction is very serious, but there are times we just don't have the information and we really need that information and we can't do it without you.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But holistically, I would say this.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And I've trained my assistants to do this.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Like, this was a whole change that I had to bring about starting 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's no longer necessarily just the charges, okay?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's the person.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: How did they get here?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And what is justice going to look like?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And in order to determine that, you have to look at everything.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Their family makeup, whether or not they experienced trauma before, you know, what is happening in their community.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: What has happened?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And in school, all we take, I leave nothing, no stone unturned.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: If I could get the information that's going to be helpful for me to determine what should happen with that child, I welcome it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Like, again, I want to stress, DAs are not using it to punish kids.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We're using it to make sure that we can do something about it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The way the law is written now, certain things we can get the information only as far as bail and sentencing.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, that's crazy, right?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Because all the stuff in between is what really matters.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Even if they're in detention, if things are going better for them, it may be a point where we could say, well, if this particular program or this community

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: organization will help or this family needs have changed and therefore the circumstances of the child has changed, maybe we can have them, you know, leave detention and go into the community and still be monitored.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But if I don't get that information, I can only use it for bail, which means to punish them, right?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Or sentencing after they're convicted, then that defeats the purpose.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just one more question.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether the DA's office experiences difficulty getting names of youth held in detention from ACS. Clark says they know their own case names but not whether youth remain detained; she recalls the COVID-era effort when the city provided lists for release review.
chapters.title: Farías asks about ACS detention lists and long pending cases

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Prosecutors have reported difficulty getting the names of young people held in detention from ACS.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Information needed to identify and prioritize long pending cases.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Has your office experienced this?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And what information do you currently receive from ACS?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And what do you need?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Look, we know the names of the kids.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I mean, we know what cases we're carrying.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The thing is, I don't know if they're still in detention.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And we won't know that because the court dates vary.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Some are long-term, some are short-term.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We don't necessarily know.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We have to keep in touch with the defense attorney.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Look, they have a heavy caseload just like we do.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So things get caught up in between.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: If we, like for Rikers, during COVID, you talked about how we did it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: This is how we did it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The city came to us and said, these are the people that are here.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Can you look at these cases and tell us whether or not you would agree to them being released?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And we did it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We looked at those cases.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We looked at the circumstance.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Now, we didn't agree on all of them.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Some of them were able to be released.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Some of them were not.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But at least we knew what to look at.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Like, you want me to look at all my cases?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I have a lot of cases.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But if we want to prioritize this, if we really want to reduce the population, then we need to work together.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Tell me who you want me to consider.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And I will look at it, and we can move forward from there.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But without it, I can't do it.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Because what happens is, you know, when we get the case, we immediately, when a person is detained, we have to consider whether we're going to be presenting that case before a grand jury.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We have 144, let's say 120 to 144 hours to do that, okay?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: So at that point, when we're making that decision with respect to whether we're going to present a case,

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: case in the grand jury, we want to know who this person is.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We want to know at that point what's going on with that person.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But after we indict the case, if we indict it, if the grand jury decides that an indictment is appropriate and we present the case to court, we come into court shortly after, you know, maybe a day or so after we do a six-day appearance in front of the youth part judge.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Where we discuss whether that case should be retained in part or not.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Because even if the case is indicted, it could still go to family court.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But we then argue in front of the court, this case should be retained in the part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Because this is a serious offense.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: This is not something that should be going to family court.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But at that point, we start talking to defense and saying to defense, look, we need information from you because we need to understand what's going on with the child.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We also try to reach out to other partners to try to understand, is the child...

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: If the child is still detained, what's going on in the detention center and what's going to happen going forward in the detention center.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day, if the child has needs and we find out that the child has a mental issue or substance use disorder or has trauma

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: in the family, situations that have happened in that child's life that require attention, we offer that not only to the court but to defense counsel, to anyone who will hear so that they can help that child out while that child is in detention.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Meanwhile, we're trying to converse with defense attorney to try to get a disposition on the cases as early as possible, but oftentimes we get nowhere with defense.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We have no information, additional information to help us.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: understand what to do with respect to the case and we basically just have an indictment or an indicted case in front of the court, at which point the court asks us, what are we doing with the case?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And at that point, we can't do it by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We need defense, we need everybody to help so that we can reach these types of dispositions.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And I just want to add one thing.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: The reason why I built the Youth Justice Bureau is because that we were backed up with cases.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: There wasn't the proper amount of attention that needed to be taken for the case.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And I have to own some of that as well because of all of the responsibilities of my assistants.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I said, let me build a team who are focused on this population that understand what the needs are and how important it is to move these things forward.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So what I'm dealing with right now is the backlog that I had.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So some of them have been in there a long time and didn't get the attention that it needed up front.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I'm dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But as the case is coming in, we're doing it a lot quicker because we know how we need to approach it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So it's a combination of both.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I have a number of council members who have questions for the DA, so we're actually going to have to move on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We have Councilmember Hanif, then we have Ressler, and then Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And Councilmember Sanchez and Brewer have joined us.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shahana Hanif asks about Youth Justice Bureau staffing and funding and about detention versus community alternatives. Edouard says the bureau has nine ADAs, three leaders, and about eight support staff; he says judges decide retention and ankle monitoring, and more youth are being placed on ankle monitors.
chapters.title: Hanif questions Youth Justice Bureau staffing and ankle monitors

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Stevens, and thank you, D.A.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Clark, for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shahanahini from Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I wanted to know a little bit more about the youth.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Justice Bureau, what's the staffing levels of the Bureau and funding for the Bureau?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm grateful to learn more about that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And would love to know, you know, how often is your office requesting detention rather than community-based alternatives?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, I was shocked to learn that the electronic ankle monitoring

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: costs are so high that it is actually, young people are not using or able to afford, and so they're likely to be detained.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you talk a little bit more about the options in terms of remaining detained and being

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: housed but with an ankle monitor?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Yeah, with respect to the Bureau, right now we have nine assistant district attorneys and we have a leadership team of three.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And we have support staff that is professional staff, legal support staff of about eight people helping us out.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: That's what the Bureau is.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: It's 19, 20 people managing all of the cases in two youth parts, okay?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: That's the structure of the Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: With respect to your question regarding retention and ankle monitors, what's happening now is the cases that are being retained are really simply only the cases that must be retained.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Because remember, a judge is reviewing it.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: It's not the district attorney's office deciding to retain a case.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We decide to move towards retention, but we bring that in front of the court, and the court is...

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: is the one that's reviewing what it is that we have as evidence and whether that evidence supports us retaining that case in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: So the judge decides that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So you're saying the judge is deciding who is staying at Horizons or Crossroads?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: No, deciding who's staying in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Now, with respect to detention, when the person is in custody,

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: versus when the person is on ankle monitor, that's a different decision.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Well, the judge decides all of that too, but when the child goes to Horizons or Crossroads and whether they're in custody and how long they remain there and what we know about what goes on in custody, that's a different conversation.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: But with respect to a different conversation in the sense that

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Horizons and Crossroads obviously monitor what's going on with the residents that they have inside of their facilities.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We're not involved and engaged in that on a daily basis, and we don't know what's going on with that, which is what Judge Clark was talking about.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We don't have information on a daily basis with respect to who's detained and who's not, because at any given moment, somebody could make bail.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And when that person makes bail, we don't necessarily get that information.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: That said, in terms of ankle monitor, the judge decides whether the person should be on ankle monitor or not.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: And in our jurisdiction, we're finding that the judge, the judges, we have two of them, are deciding to place a lot more people on ankle monitor than previously.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: We're seeing a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: more often now than ever before, where they have an opportunity to be in the community, but on an ankle monitor, as opposed to being in custody in Horizons or Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But it's also the city determines how many ankle monitors there are for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Remember, we're not just talking about the Bronx, we're talking about all five boroughs, and there's only a certain amount of ankle monitors for the city.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So we're talking about adults as well as youth.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But as far as the staffing is concerned, you want to address really who is the staff.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: So the DA was very careful about creating this bureau and making sure the expertise was in place to know not just how to prosecute cases, but also how to deal with these issues surrounding children.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: So, for instance, Marceau has extensive experience in his background.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: I worked not only in this area before, but also with the law department, the juvenile delinquency and their family court division.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: I was a hearing officer for special education cases as well for the city.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: But our staff want to be with us.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: We have teachers.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: We have people who worked for ACS before, people who were in gun advocacy prevention efforts before.

utterances.speaker: Ginger James
utterances.text: So everybody has a special reason for being in the Bureau and a special expertise they bring in.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what concrete steps the DA's office is taking to reduce pre-conviction incarceration. Edouard begins describing quick dispositions in retained youth part cases, but Stevens cuts in because of time and moves to the next council member.
chapters.title: Hanif asks DA actions to reduce pre-conviction incarceration

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Because I don't have a lot of time, I'll follow up just to learn a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: But could you share now just what other concrete steps the DA's team is taking to reduce the number of young people incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: before they've been convicted?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Say that again, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's the DA's office doing to reduce the number of young people incarcerated before they're convicted?

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Well, very quickly, and I'll let my colleague add on to this, what we're doing immediately is to address

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: the situation very, very, very quickly with respect to disposition of a case when it's before us.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: In other words, once the case is retained in the youth part, because remember, we only handle cases that are retained in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Edouard
utterances.text: Once they're retained in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have to move on because we have a number of council members and we haven't got to the administration, so we have to move on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The next council member we have is Council Member Ressler and then Council Member Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler asks whether assistant district attorneys understand diversion programs and alternatives. Clark says they know some but not all, and supports Chair Stevens' guide legislation; she also calls for evaluation of program effectiveness.
chapters.title: Restler asks if ADAs know diversion programs and alternatives

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will try not to.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is this working?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll try not to take full advantage of the time to keep Chair Stevens on schedule.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Gay Clark, it's great to see you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you feel that your assistant DAs have a comprehensive understanding of

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the diversion programs and alternatives that are available for young people instead of detention?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I think that we do know what is available.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We don't know everything.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So there's, like anything else, there's a lot of programs, there's a lot of resources, but unless you know about them, we can't take advantage of them.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So there needs to be a concerted effort, and we've tried to do that before.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I held a summit of all youth justice stakeholders to say, okay, you do this, you do that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Let's put everything together so we know what is available, what the requirements are, so we can take advantage of that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So the answer is yes and no.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We know what we know, but we don't know what we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just want to underscore that to say that I think Chair Stevens'legislation in particular would be really helpful, that there be an up-to-date, real-time guide that's available of all of the different programs that we could be placing people into instead of detention.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I hope that's something that you're supporting.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I do support that.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: And with that, also said that not only to just know those resources, to make sure that you evaluate them to well, to make sure that they're effective.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Because there's a lot of folks out here putting up tents saying they do this, that, and the third, and they're not really, you know, producing what they say they're going to be.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: But I 100% support that effort.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: 100% programs should be evidence-based and effective.

chapters.summary: Restler lists Adams administration cuts to Department of Probation programs including IMPACT, Next Steps, Arches, and ICM. Clark says the cuts mean fewer resources but not necessarily more detention, and says Probation resources need to be restored.
chapters.title: Restler questions Probation cuts and resulting resource gaps

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, one of the hallmarks of the Adams administration was the hollowing out of the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we saw program after program just eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: $5 million in cuts to evidence-based programs for at-risk young adults, such as the IMPACT program, $700,000 cut, $2.6 million cut to Next Steps, $1.6 million cut to Arches.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We saw the ICM program, Intensive Community Monitoring Program, gutted.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I could keep going, but you got the drift.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Has, we have not yet really seen those programs replaced.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So do you feel the difference?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you notice the fact that we can't rely on, we haven't been able over these last number of years to rely on the Department of Probation?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is anything changing?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you feel like there's a gap there that's leading to more detention as a result?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I can't say that it's leading to more detention, but I could say it's leading to less resources that we could use that would be helpful in determining whether or not somebody could be detained.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Look, the Department of Probation is a massive agency that does great work.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I've worked alongside them all my life, starting as an assistant DA, 16 years as a judge, sentencing people to probation, and now 10 years with the DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: They play a vital role in this space, and I want to see them get as many resources as possible that they can use to help us with that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You want to call out any specific programs that were cut by the Adams administration and Commissioner Holmes that you think need to be restored?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't, you would know better than me.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I don't know exactly every single one.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I just know the resources were cut, and we need them back.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We need them back.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I don't care who was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We need them.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I told the chair that I wouldn't use my whole time, so I'm yielding it back for the first time ever.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Pierina Ana Sanchez says she is concerned about secure detention and thanks Clark for Bronx Restore and Project Rise. She asks about conversations with the new deputy mayor for community safety; Clark says they have met and she is encouraged.
chapters.title: Sanchez confirms Bronx Restore funding and asks about deputy mayor talks

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The first time for everything.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We're not going there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I won't be able to stay for the whole hearing, so I just wanted to take a moment to state on the record that Chair Stevens is not alone.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: own, but as evidenced by the council members who are here today, as evidenced by so many of us who have gone to Horizons, who've gone to Crossroads with her and are with her in this place of deep concern about secure detention in our city and our kids.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Bronx DA, I count myself as so fortunate to be able to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for the efforts to get us Bronx Restore over on Fordham Road in the 46th Precinct and in the 40th.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I just wanted to ask a question, just confirming on the record, the funding for Bronx Restore came from the governor?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So, you know, just want to make sure that we continue to work together.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm already asking her for, you know, we got twin grants for the West Bronx in terms of Project Restore and the Bronx Restore and the Project Rise, both in the West Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm already trying to make sure that we get her committed to funding it for another two years, even after the initial two.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So thank you for your work.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then my question was just, how have your conversations been with the new deputy mayor of community safety?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you all talking about funding sources for the innovative work that you're doing?

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: We've met with them, and, you know, it's a process.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: It's a new leadership, you know.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I've been the DA 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: I've had four mayors, three mayors, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: How many DOC commissioners, six police commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Like, you know, you've got to give people a minute.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: So I am encouraged by what I'm hearing from the Office of...

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: community safety and willing to partner with them in any way I can to make sure we could do all that we can to get the Bronx safe, to keep the Bronx safe.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you, DA.

utterances.speaker: Darcel D. Clark
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Stevens thanks DA Clark for testifying and says the committee will now call the administration. She asks council staff to swear in the administration panelists, and there is brief procedural chatter.
chapters.title: Stevens thanks DA Clark and calls administration panel

chapters.summary: ACS Commissioner Rebecca Jones Gaston introduces herself and the administration panel. Panelists include Nancy Ginsberg, Stacey Desmore, Desmond Moore, Miriam Popper, Ray Toomer, Stephanie Gendell, Robert Asubio, and Devin Bailey.
chapters.title: ACS Commissioner Gaston introduces administration panel

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I'm Rebecca Jones-Gaston, the Commissioner for the Administration for Children's Services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I am joined at the days with Nancy Ginsberg, the Deputy Commissioner for the Division of Youth and Family Justice, which oversees our Juvenile Justice Continuum.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I am also joined at the days with my colleague, Stacey Desmore.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Desmond Moore, the Deputy Commissioner for Juvenile Operations at the Department of Probation, and Miriam Popper, the Senior Advisor

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: for Youth Justice at the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice, who will be available for Q&A.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: In addition, we have Ray Toomer and Stephanie Gendel from ACS, and Robert Asubio and...

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Devin Bailey from DOP also available and joining us for Q&A.

chapters.summary: Gaston states the administration's commitment to reduce the number of young people in care and improve conditions for those ordered into detention. She thanks the committee for visiting Horizon and Crossroads and thanks ACS staff and partners.
chapters.title: Gaston states commitment to reduce detention and improve conditions

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We are pleased to be here for today's hearing and look forward to sharing our efforts to reduce the number of young people in our care.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: While improving the conditions for youth ordered held by the court into detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Together, we have an unwavering

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: commitment to provide youth and families with services, supports, and interventions that put youth on a pathway to success.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Our goal is always for youth to thrive in their homes and communities, for those young people whose paths have led them to secure detention facilities,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We are committed to not only their safety and security, but to providing them with the tools, skills, and opportunities to put them on the pathway to a successful adulthood.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Stevens and the members of the committee for holding today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We also want to express our appreciation to you and your fellow council members for visiting both Horizon and Crossroads to have a better understanding of the operational aspects of the facilities and to meet the young people and the staff.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I also want to thank the ACS staff in our secure detention centers.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: They spend each and every day providing compassionate support and care for the safety and well-being of the young people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: These staff, along with the Bellevue Mental Health Team, H&H Medical Team, the New York City Public School Team, and all of the providers and volunteers are committed to ensuring the young people in our custody

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: have what they need to thrive and make good decisions when they leave detention, regardless of where the next stop in their journey may be.

chapters.summary: Gaston says ACS operates Horizon and Crossroads and that admissions, age, length of stay, and charge severity have increased since 2022. As of October 23, the census was 352 youth, with 178 at Crossroads and 174 at Horizon; 346 were charged as adolescent or juvenile offenders.
chapters.title: Gaston presents secure detention census and Raise the Age data

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS Opera

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: two secure detention centers, Horizon in the Bronx, Crossroads in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Since 2022, after the implementation of Raise the Age and the impact of the pandemic, the number of young people admitted to detention has increased.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And the age, length of stay, and severity of charges faced by those youth has also increased.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Specifically, on October 23rd, our census, the census was 352 youth, with 178 housed at Crossroads, 174 at Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And of those 352 youth, eight were girls and the remainder were boys.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Just 26 of those young people were age 15 and younger.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The median age of the young people in secure detention is 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: 346 youth were charged as adolescent offenders or juvenile offenders in the youth part of the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And six youth have cases solely in family court.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: On one hand, this shows that raise the age is working.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Judges are not holding young people charged with lower level crimes in secure detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: On the other hand, we have seen our detention census increase.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And the needs of the young people who remain in care with ACS remain longer, and the reasons they are in secure detention.

chapters.summary: Gaston outlines Mamdani administration efforts to expand community-based alternatives and intensive monitoring. She says ACS invested an additional $12.2 million in alternatives, is expediting discharges, and is working to establish non-secure detention as a step-down option.
chapters.title: Gaston outlines community alternatives and step-down efforts

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration is taking many steps to help us meet those needs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We all want young people to get services and supports that they need and that their families need, and to get these in the community when possible.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS's Community-Based Alternatives Continuum

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: provides a range of support services to over 3,000 youth and their families each year.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: To increase the availability of these services, starting in fiscal year 26 and growing in fiscal year 2027, ACS invested an additional $12.2 million

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: in our community-based alternatives to expand the support available for youth and help prevent detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration is pursuing every avenue possible to meet the needs of the youth in the community and to ultimately reduce the census and detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: This includes additional investments in the community-based services and intensive monitoring that enables youth to remain in the community.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: In addition, the Mamdani administration has focused on efforts to expedite youth discharge from detention by working closely with the court system and court partners.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We have been collaborating to establish ACS's non-secure detention programs as an option for judges to step down youth who are doing well in security.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: detention to a less restrictive environment.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We have also been coordinating with the state so that youth that have been sentenced are more expeditiously transferred.

chapters.summary: Gaston says Horizon and Crossroads were built for fewer youth and shorter stays, leaving more youth than bedrooms. She says youth sleep in common areas, classrooms, or the chapel, and describes expedited construction of the Horizon annex and Crossroads auxiliary housing.
chapters.title: Gaston describes overcapacity, sleeping arrangements, and construction

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: While our goal is to reduce the number of young people in detention, we must also ensure youth receive the highest quality of care in the safest environment possible.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Horizon and Crossroads were built for younger youth with shorter lengths of stay,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: and to have 123 and 122 bedrooms respectively.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: With a census of 352 youth, this means that currently we have more young people than bedrooms and have had to identify alternative housing options.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Every young person, including those not assigned to an individual bedroom, has a bed with full bedding and a place to store their belongings.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Most of these youth sleep in the common area of the hall for which they are assigned.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: While a smaller number sleep in classrooms or in the chapel until an appropriate hall can be identified.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Every youth, regardless of sleeping arrangement, has access to education, recreation, programming, case management, and hygiene.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The census also impacts the availability of space for programming, services, education,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: and workforce development, as well as safe movement throughout the facilities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Thanks to the Mamdani's administration commitment to improving the quality of care, ACS and the Department of Design and Construction, DDC,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: are also in the process of expediting the completion of an annex at Horizon and auxiliary housing at Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Construction of the Horizon Annex is underway and with the expedited timeline should be completed by the end of 2027 rather than the previously anticipated 2029.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The Horizon Annex will include 56 bedrooms, 8 classrooms including 2 trade workshops,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: an industrial kitchen, multiple dining areas, a secondary health clinic, and a new three-story exercise pavilion.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is also working with DDC on the plans to construct auxiliary housing at Crossroads, which will add 28 bedrooms and two classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Over the summer, ACS worked with the School Construction Authority to expedite the addition of trailers to create two new classrooms at Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is incredibly appreciative of the efforts made to bring these online so quickly and look forward to the new classrooms opening in the next few weeks.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I want to be clear that this is not a situation where if we build it, they will come.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: While we are working across systems to divert, prevent, and serve youth outside of detention, the fact of the matter is we are currently over capacity.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: It is our obligation to ensure that youth who are already in our care have access to quality services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: That is what these projects aim to do.

chapters.summary: Gaston says ACS has increased searches, procured handheld and mobile x-ray scanners, and added entrance and exit scanning technology. She says ACS has hired 166 youth development specialists and 52 special officers, and expanded crisis intervention and threat assessment training.
chapters.title: Gaston details contraband searches, scanners, and staffing hires

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is committed to the safety and security of both youth and staff.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Preventing, identifying, and removing contraband is an essential piece to safety.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We increased the number and frequency of searches and have procured cutting-edge handheld and mobile x-ray scanners to assist in finding any contraband hidden in opaque surfaces or items.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We have added new scanning technology at the entrances and exits.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: As well as for use throughout the facility.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We've implemented new protocols to ensure this equipment is utilized safely and consistently.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is working closely with OMB to ensure our facilities are sufficiently staffed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Since the start of the Momdani administration, we have hired many new staff for detention, including 166 YDS, Youth Development Specialists, and 52 Special Officers.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is focused on recruiting a workforce that reflects the communities we serve.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Recruitment starts with promoting ACS civil service careers through targeted outreach at educational institutions, community-based organizations, and job fairs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Over the past year, ACS has participated in more than 110 hiring and recruitment events.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: As part of our ongoing commitment to supporting staff, we've expanded access to practical skills-based training.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: To date, 67 staff members have participated in advanced crisis intervention training, which strengthens their verbal de-escalation skills, crisis communication, and incident management skills.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: An additional 19 staff participated in the Vigilance Threat Assessment and Crisis Communication Training, which provides structured tools for assessing higher risk situations, making sound

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: and defensible decisions, and intervening safely when needed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Additional training sessions are planned.

chapters.summary: Gaston highlights education, workforce, and youth programming in detention. She says ACS expanded GED and college options, has 39 students in college, provides tutoring through Children's Village and Youth Justice Network, and offers trades certifications and arts and recreational programs.
chapters.title: Gaston highlights education, workforce, and youth programming

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Our most important work is giving young people the tools and skills that they need to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Our focus on youth development includes a combination of services, education, workforce development, arts and music programming, recreation, youth-led cognitive behavior therapy, and mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS has been very intentional in creating an environment that embraces and supports education.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: As the population in secure detention is older and includes young people ages 18 to 20 who are not legally required to attend school,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS has increased access to high school equivalency options.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Many of our youth in detention who have graduated or received their GEDs are now enrolled in college courses.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Through the Hostos Community College and the Borough of Manhattan Community College.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Earning transferable college credits.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: This fall, we have 39 students enrolled in college classes.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Tutoring is beneficial for many, as the youth benefit from individualized academic support,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS's contracted workforce partners, the Children's Village, the Youth Justice Network, provide on-site tutoring four days a week for 40 to 50 youth during the school day, after school,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: and on holidays.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Tutors work with the same students, building strong relationships that support academic achievements for the young people.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Recognizing the importance of vocational opportunities and their appeal to the young people, ACS has developed workforce partnerships that allow young youth to explore and earn certificates in a variety of trades.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Options include building maintenance programs, paintings, spackling, taping, electrical skills, personal trainer training, culinary arts, entrepreneurship, and small business development,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: as well as barbering courses and podcast engineering.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: OSHA and HVAC accreditations are also available.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Informed by the input from the youth in our custody, ACS has strengthened programming options both to keep young people engaged and to broaden the depth of their experiences and opportunities for learning.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Programming

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: places a strong emphasis on leadership development, creative expression, conflict resolution, and healthy decision making.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Current offerings include music production, improv, visual arts, filmmaking, fitness training, yoga,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: culinary and hospitality skills, restorative justice and violence interruption services, and therapeutic horticulture.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: In addition, ACS's program

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Gram counselors provide daily engagement activities.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Youth also engage in culturally responsive, theme-based programming, most recently for Hispanic Heritage Month and Breast Cancer Awareness Month in October.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The artwork produced

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: by young people has been displayed in public art shows in Harlem, the Bronx, and most recently in a gallery in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We are including some of the postcards featuring the murals created by youth in Crossroads.

chapters.summary: Gaston describes medical and mental health services provided by H&H and Bellevue. She says H&H provides 24/7 medical and dental care and Bellevue provides trauma-informed mental health teams, with roughly 80 to 90% of detained youth voluntarily engaged in mental health services.
chapters.title: Gaston describes H&H medical and Bellevue mental health services

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Finally, critical to the success of the young people is the provision of high quality health and mental health services, which are provided by H&H and Bellevue respectively.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: H&H provides comprehensive medical and dental care in secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Medical services are available 24-7 for all youth housed in secure and non-secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And includes initial and comprehensive assessments, episodic visits, routine care, as well as scheduling and coordination of specialty appointments.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Bellevue Juvenile Mental Health Services provides comprehensive, trauma-informed mental health services

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: with a team of psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed clinical social workers, psychiatric nurse practitioners, and creative artists, creative arts therapists.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: All youth have ongoing access to mental health treatment provided by Bellevue, and typically approximately 80 to 90% of the youth in detention are engaged in mental health services on a voluntary basis.

chapters.summary: Gaston comments on the legislation before the committee. She supports Intro 447's alternatives guide, appreciates Intro 629's intent while assessing confidentiality issues, and says ACS supports annual anti-trafficking training under Intro 977, noting 2025 training reach.
chapters.title: Gaston comments on Intro 447, Intro 629, and Intro 977

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The proposed legislation, 447-2026, sponsored by Chair Stevens, would require ACS, in consultation with the Department of Youth and Community Development, DOP, and Mach J,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: to develop a guide containing information about available alternative to detention and alternative to incarceration programs.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And then distribute it to judges, attorneys, public defender organizations, youth advocates, and district attorneys.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS agrees with and appreciates the Council's interest in ensuring court partners are aware of the programs available to serve youth in community.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the Council and our partner agencies on legislation to ensure this critical information is readily available for all of our partners.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Introduce Bill 629-2026, sponsored by Councilmember Ressler, would create teams

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: comprised of city agencies, service providers, to review factors such as charges, mental health needs, and psychosocial conditions related to the youth's circumstances and consult with

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: case management related to the youth circumstances, consulting with case management, programmatic and education staff for every youth in detention after seven days and every six months thereafter.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: This to identify youth in detention who could be subject for early case resolution or release pre-trial.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS appreciates the intent of this bill and agrees that no youth who does not need to be in detention should be in detention.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS is working closely with the law department to assess the proposal's interaction with confidentiality protections in existing law.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the council on this proposal as well.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Introduce proposal 977-2026, sponsored by Council Member Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Would require ACS and DYCD mandate annual staff trainings related to identifying sexually exploited youth.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS shared information about our array of trainings at a hearing in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: As an update, in 2025, ACS provided 90 trainings, which filled over 16,000 training seats, mostly virtual, some in person, and some individuals may have been counted more than once.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Over 3,000 people participated in these trainings that specifically addressed ACS anti-trafficking policy and screening procedures.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS appreciates the importance of this type of training and the value of an annual mandated training.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: ACS again looks forward to working with the council on this legislation.

chapters.summary: Gaston concludes by thanking the City Council, City Hall colleagues, ACS teams, and partners. She says much work remains to reduce the detention census and improve care, and thanks the young people in ACS custody.
chapters.title: Gaston concludes administration testimony with thanks

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: In conclusion, I want to thank the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: My City Hall colleagues, the teams working with my panelists and the ACS team for their ongoing commitment to young people.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: While much work remains to be done,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: both to reduce the detention census and strengthen the conditions of care, I remain very moved by the deep passion and commitment I see each and every day as I visit Crossroads and Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Please know to our teams,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: and our partners, I see you and all the work that you do to enhance the safety, security, and well-being of all of the young people in our care.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And to the young people in our custody, please know that there are countless people committed to you and to helping you thrive.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm actually going to do something I typically don't do, which is allow my colleagues to go first because we have a number of folks who are here and I want to make sure that questions get asked.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm going to start with our public advocate.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You can go second.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Oh, councilman.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yep.

chapters.summary: Council Member Sandy Nurse asks about timelines for the September 15 announcement, working groups, and meetings with district attorneys and court liaisons. Miriam Popper describes the Youth Justice Working Group, five subgroups, and borough-based meetings with ADAs, defenders, and judges.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about September 15 plan timelines and working groups

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So my questions are really related to the September 15th announcement.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm just like going through your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm trying to get more detail of kind of what these pieces are and how they're going to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So really just curious about what are the timelines for each of the policy pieces?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: That were mentioned in the September 15th announcement.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So, you know, where are we at in terms of status of some of them?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I have questions around when, I'm going to just say them all, when will the working groups start meeting?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Have they started meeting?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Are you all currently meeting with the DAs and the court liaisons?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And how are those conversations going?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And then I just have some other questions about the status of the hiring, of the numbers you presented, the 56 youth development specialists, the 85 staff for emergency response, where we at in terms of recruitment and onboarding those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I'll go back through, I'm just throwing a bunch out for now.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So I'm gonna start by passing it over to my colleague, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Popper, to respond to the first few questions.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for those.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So thinking about the working group,

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So our Youth Justice Working Group, which is one of our overarching strategies to approach youth justice more broadly, really from prevention through reentry.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: The primary group has met once, our stakeholder group met in the summer, and our next meeting will be roughly every quarter, so coming up in November.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: That group will be meeting again.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And then the work to really move the needle is happening within subgroups.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: There's five subgroups focused on prevention, in-custody programming, detention reduction, court-based programming, and reentry.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And so those groups are meeting roughly every month to every six weeks.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: We've had a meeting of almost all of them now, and the rest are coming up in this next week or two that haven't met yet.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And then in terms of meeting with the DAs, the court liaisons, part of the population reduction

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: group that's going to be meeting, sorry, that has been meeting.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: We've been talking to ADAs that are in the youth part, public defenders in the youth parts, the judges overseeing the youth parts, meeting with each of those individually and then as borough-based groups as well.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And so those meetings have been happening now for a number of months, and we've had...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And how many...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So you've been...

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: What's the frequency of those meetings with the DAs?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So with the DAs, for example, that's every six weeks.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: weeks that we're meeting with them as a group citywide and then as well as in borough as part of the borough-based groups.

chapters.summary: Stevens interjects that district attorneys told her they had only two meetings mostly about secure detention information. She asks how the meetings reduce the population; Popper says the meetings share new investments, programs, and case-delay issues.
chapters.title: Stevens challenges value of DA meetings in reducing population

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can I just interject really quickly because one of the things when I spoke with the DAs they said that they've had two meetings and

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: it was more information and it was about telling them about secure detention so I'm just trying to get a better understanding of how are these meetings helping meet the crisis that we're in and reducing the population so I'm trying to understand how are these meetings helping that because that's

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: my experience is that's not what's been happening.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as we've talked about, one of the important things is getting information to all the court stakeholders about the new investments that are coming online, about the programs that exist.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And so we're very excited about building out a resource guide for each borough to make sure they know about that.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: But we're also doing that in the meetings.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So we've, at one of our meetings,

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: our meetings we talked about some of the new investments that were mentioned in that press release what's going to be coming online we've had probation come to talk about the new ICM connect program which is part of our population reduction direction strategy

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: and so in those meetings we always leave time to say

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: We want to be hearing from you about what are the other things that are affecting case delay right now that we can be working with our city partners on and the other court partners as well.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: You know, are there issues, you know,

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: getting discovery from NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And so my understanding is every six weeks, you all are sharing what you have, the resources, investments, you're leaving space for them, and you're saying, what can we do?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And are there concrete proposals coming out from that side?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So we are developing concrete proposals as we speak to each of these partners.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And, for example, we've been working on, you know, one of the aspects is on case delay.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And so thinking about how can we make sure that mitigation reports are getting to the court sooner.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: That's one of the things that is holding up cases.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And so making sure that 18B attorneys, for example, have social work support.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And mitigation specialists on board for every single case that starts in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So the things coming out of these conversations, we're able to turn into policy recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Chair, I just wanted to get my original, my other question asked first.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you for the recounting of the DA meetings and the court liaisons.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks for timelines on expanding alternatives, family-based treatment, ICM Connect, and non-secure detention. Popper says Families Rising and Exalt contracts are with the comptroller, will register within four weeks, and new tracks start November 16; Deanna Logan describes the Bronx ICM Connect pilot with 150 slots.
chapters.title: Nurse asks timelines on ATI, family treatment, ICM, and non-secure

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: In terms of the timeline for policies, so the bullets that I have here is expanding alternatives to detention, expanding family-based treatment, launching the intensive community monitoring, which I'd love for you all to detail what that means exactly.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And the ICM Connect expanding non-secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Specifically, I was very curious about the youth continuum of care.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So where are we on these in terms of getting them off the ground?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Yes, so the two ATI programs are mentioned in that, Families Rising and Exalt.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: These are the programs we heard from the court stakeholders were most useful for reducing specifically the secure detention population.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Their contracts are both with the comptroller right now, so they will be registered within four weeks.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: They'll be backdated to October 1st, and the providers are already in the process of hiring.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: We expect with both of those contracts, they'll be bringing in new young people for these new tracks starting November 16th for both of the ATI programs.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And the family-based treatment?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: The family-based treatment is one of the ATI programs, Families Rising, a functional family therapy program.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, and the launching of the intensive community monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This is DOP.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: Begin the Intensive Community Mind ICM Connect on November 16th.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We're going to be beginning a pilot in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We've already met with some of the Bronx stakeholders with regards to that.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We have the staff that's available.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We're starting to have some implementation meetings.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We're going over policy.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: practice, how we're going to start accepting those young people.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: So we are working behind the scenes.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: It may not be in public, but we're working behind the scenes to be prepared and ready to take those young people because we understand that it's a crisis and we are here as partners to work in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And this release said it was for 100 to support additional, an additional 150 young people.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: Yes, for those that are in secure detention from Horizon and Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And so what would be the total then for everybody?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Is it just that additional funding is specific for that $150,000, or is that on top of any other?

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: So for the ICE Intensive Community Monitoring Connect, it's going to be 150 young people.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We want to keep those caseloads to about 10 per PO because we want to make sure that it's intensive, that we're intentional, and that we are engaging those young people as well as the parents, right, and making sure that they are

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: getting what they need as well.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: But I just want to emphasize that we also still have ICM, regular intensive community monitoring, that is available for family court and youth.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: part and we may be a little bit over capacity, but we still take kids.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: We don't turn anyone away and that is available as an alternative for the courts.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: And we have staff that's identified and we continue to restructure and bring it back to where it was.

utterances.speaker: Deanna Logan
utterances.text: It's available and if the courts for those young people that are ROR or that are at arraignment, it's available.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks whether the 56 youth development specialists and 85 emergency response staff are hired. Gaston and Gendell say 56 YDS were hired between June and September, 166 YDS have been hired since January, and the 85 special officer and supervisor positions are still being recruited.
chapters.title: Nurse asks about hiring youth development and emergency staff

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, and then my last question was just about where we were in terms of the 56 youth development specialists and the 85 staff.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How far along are we on recruitment and onboarding?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So I'll start and then I'll turn it over to DC at Gundell is those are the staff that have been hired, right?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Oh, they've already been hired.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: They've already been hired.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: We are in a continuous kind of hiring mode where there's ongoing recruitment, ongoing hiring and onboarding, and then the training, obviously, that's connected to that.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: The ability to make sure that we have the staff that we need is really critical.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And the partnerships that we're getting and the support that we're getting across city agencies has been really critical.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So just to clarify, all, just because the way it's written in some of these things, it seemed like it was like an aspiration.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So are all 56 youth development specialists hired that are in this announcement?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So the 56 youth development specialists were hired.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Between June and September.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Actually, for the calendar year of 2026, it is 166 thus far.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And the 85 staff for emergency response?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: The 85 staff for emergency response?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Yes, those are currently being recruited and hired now.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, so that's still not fully.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a new kind of body of work and team that we've created, and so we're recruiting for that currently.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay, and do you know how many you've started to recruit or?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's still in the early days?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: So that's still in the early days because that's new, and we're in the process of doing the recruiting for the emergency response.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: It's a different title.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: Those aren't youth development specialists.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: Those are special officers and special officer supervisors.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: And the commissioner said exactly what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: To just be clear, everything was sort of a point in time.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: So the press release 56 YDS are already hired, and those are from June to September.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: But since January, we've hired 166 YDS.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This is clarifying.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you so much.
