chapters.summary: Stevens says the situation does not feel treated like a crisis, noting the September 15 announcement and November program start dates. She asks whether the state waiver was revoked so youth can no longer sleep in unconventional areas; Gaston says it is absolutely a crisis.
chapters.title: Stevens presses administration on crisis urgency and revoked waiver

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to the public advocate, but I have a question because I just, even with some of the timelines, I'm just confused.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is this not a crisis that we have so many young people in secure detention?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because it doesn't feel that way.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because this announcement was on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We're talking about the community partnership stuff happening in November, and it just seems very much like not a crisis, especially when...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The waiver is revoked from the state, correct?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because the waiver from the state is removed, so kids aren't allowed to sleep in unconventional areas anymore, correct?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So first of all, it absolutely is a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And I think what you hear and will continue to hear is the variety of things that we are putting in place and investing in across the continuum.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Prevention efforts to serve kids in the community as well as the ability for our probation partners to have

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: in community monitoring and the the work with the the court system and our other partners across that the

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: and i hear you but this isn't new when the administration came in this was happening and so why is it now that it's a crisis because it's the waiver was revoked because i'm confused and that's why i'm frustrated because this isn't a new issue

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: and it's coming off as if this is something that's new and I've been ringing the alarm for three years so I'm frustrated because I'm sitting here and we're talking about

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: plans that we're implementing now when this has not been a priority since January, as it should have been, like we've been calling for.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm just a little frustrated with, like, it doesn't feel like a sense of urgency.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it to Public Advocate so he can ask.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: His questions, because I did say I was going to let my colleagues go first, so I'm going to shut up again.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: No, I appreciate your questions and your passion with this.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It's welcome.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner and et al.

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Williams asks whether youth 18 and older in detention are being helped to vote. Nancy Ginsberg says ACS has held voter education events and 71 youth are registered, but she does not have the number eligible or whether they voted and will follow up.
chapters.title: Williams asks about voting among detained youth

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: First, there's a lot of young people who are 18 and over in detentions.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So I want to know if you are getting folks who are eligible to vote to be able to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is that happening?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have had events to educate our young people on becoming voters.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We currently, in our current group of young people, we have 71 young people who are registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: How many people are eligible?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: I don't have that figure.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: I do know when the mayor came to visit us, many of the young people were very proud to tell him that they voted for him.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We can get back to you on how many are eligible.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And do we know how many of the 70, how many you said, 70?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: How many of them voted?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Generally, the young people who are registered do vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So we don't know?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We do or don't know if they voted.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Well, we have the upcoming election.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The last, I don't know what the number was the last time there was an election, but we can get that number to you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, I'd like to get all those numbers because there's

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We've seen correlation of people civically engaged and being more productive.

chapters.summary: Williams asks about the DA's testimony that prosecutors are not getting information. Ginsberg says the Bronx DA requested a list in July and was provided one, Brooklyn requested multiple lists and received them, and ACS has never received a request for a daily census.
chapters.title: Williams asks about DA information requests and ACS lists

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Also, the DA's mentioned information that they are saying that they're not getting.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Is that new or is that something that's longstanding?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So we received a request from the Bronx DA's office in July for a list of young people who are in our custody.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We provided that list and we never received another request from them.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have received multiple requests from the Brooklyn DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have provided multiple lists to the Brooklyn DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: When we first got the request, we had to go to OCFS, which is our oversight agency, the state oversight agency, to ask for permission to release that information.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Once we were provided permission, we provided the information to the DA's offices.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have never received a request for a daily census.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I would just add that the importance of collaboration is absolutely critical in this.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And you heard from DA Clark some of the constraints legally in regards to what we can and cannot share.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: But our commitment is to obviously go through the process that DC.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Ginsburg identified related to our state partners in the oversight body when there are requests.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: There are also reports that do go to the DA's office upon request related to court.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Just something clear based on the answer.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: You're not aware of outstanding requests that were made?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: As far as the reports about how young people are doing in detention, we regularly provide what we call adjustment reports.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The judges can order, the judges in the youth part or in family court can order adjustment reports and we provide information for court dates upon those orders.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And so if there is a request for information about how a young person in custody is doing, a request can be made for that adjustment report and it is produced to the court for the adjourned date.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Williams asks how contraband screening has changed and whether all staff go through the same screening. Gaston says everyone entering the building is screened through x-ray and other equipment, and ACS has added new entrance, exit, and handheld scanning equipment.
chapters.title: Williams questions contraband screening of staff and visitors

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And the issue of contraband is a persistent one in the city's detention centers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This is not an indictment in any one staff or all staffs, but we have seen investigations that found the staff of bringing contraband in.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We've heard reasons, some bribery, some...

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: fear, but I've actually heard sometimes it's helpful in trying to manage the staff, so I've heard a lot of different reasons.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But I just want to understand how the security

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Screenings changed when updated, and do all staff members go through the same screening?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So everyone who comes into the building goes through the screening, through the various...

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Conveyor belt, x-ray machine, the...

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I just want to, is that like mayor, commissioner on down, everyone?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Everybody, okay.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: No matter how many times you come.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And everybody goes through the exact same screening.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Has the screening been updated at any point?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So we have added, and DC Ginsburg can add some more detail, we have added over the last year additional equipment, new equipment to both the exits and entryways, as well as handheld

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: wands.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Provide that screening for anyone who's visiting the facility, but also note that the young people screening, there are some additional steps related to that just on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Williams says he is worried that if the city builds more capacity, the system will fill it, and that attention may fade once overcrowding eases. He says the focus must remain on getting youth out and ensuring programming so they leave better.
chapters.title: Williams voices concern about expansion and losing long-term focus

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And lastly, and one, it just,

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Both the staff and the folks hired there usually come from the same community, so it's always just painful to see the things that are going on in there for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I heard the response to about, I'm sure it was in there before I said it, but if they build, they will come comment.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I disagree a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think if we build it, they will come.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm not 100% sure that I'm opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My problem is I'm hoping that it is an acute situation right now.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm worried about it when it's not.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Some of the things we're trying to do is going to go away.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And that concerns me.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Obviously, it's overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I think there's ways we have to get people off.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: If we're going to build as part of a broader plan, that's possibly a thing to do.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I agree with the chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: We need to move expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: But if we get out of the crisis of the overcrowding, I'm concerned that we will lose our attention to the processes of getting kids off of the island and making sure they have the things that they need before they come on, but not the island, I'm sorry, across the horizon.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And obviously we have to work on them not getting in there, but making sure they have the programming so they come out better.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: That is my major concern.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I don't know if there's much I can say that assuages me of that because this has been a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I just wanted to put on record of what that concern is and that we have to keep our eyes on the goal.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And it's acute right now.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There's a lot of pressure on us.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I think that pressure makes people move.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: When that's relieved, it is a very huge concern of mine.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure I put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And again, thank you, Madam Chair, for all that you keep doing for young people that some people often forget about.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to take that compliment because a public advocate never gives him compliments and it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm going to take it.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I did it publicly.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I 100% agree.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I believe if they build what they were coming, that was the first thing I said when our former commissioner was here and Stephanie called me and I was like, I know you don't control the kids coming in, but once,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: because if this is a crisis and we address the crisis, this shouldn't be a need.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And we haven't addressed the crisis, which is also very frustrating.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And again, I'm running my mouth again, and I'm going to pass it off to the deputy speaker so she can ask her questions.

chapters.summary: Deputy Speaker Farías asks how ACS provides medical, mental health, educational, family-contact, and recreational services amid overcapacity. Ginsberg cites expanded Bellevue mental health funding, career readiness funding, certifications, SYEP participation, college enrollment, and graduates.
chapters.title: Farías asks how ACS delivers services amid overcapacity

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, we love when you do that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, so access to programs.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Given that the secure detention system is over capacity by roughly 130 people, how is ACS ensuring that each young person is given the attention they need?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What procedures are in place to ensure that each young person in detention is getting appropriate medical care, mental health care, educational instruction, regular contact with parents and guardians, and access to other recreational and supervised programming?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just one thing I want to say as a follow-up to that, I know you did list out all the different things that ACS is doing to provide various programs to the young people who are in detention.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But because you all are at capacity, I think we want to understand how you're able to accomplish all of that given the capacity issue.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We share your concern about meeting the needs of all our young people.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We've been working very hard to expand available services to meet those needs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have added $9.6 million to the budget of the Bellevue Juvenile Justice Mental Health Service.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have added $4 million for career and work readiness programs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have seen last year 367 of our young people

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: receive certifications in workforce development, and we are on track for over 400 young people to receive certifications this year.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We had 94 young people participate in SYEP.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have 39 young people in college and 260 young people who have taken college classes over the seven semesters since we started

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: offering college classes through the MOU with K-316.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have graduated 163 young people since 2022-2023, and we are on track to graduate more.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have periodic graduations for young people who complete their GEDs and regular graduations aligned with the school year for young people.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: who are being promoted from middle school, although we have very few of those, and high school regions graduates.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: You asked about something else, right?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, no, just you don't have a lot of space, and so it just begs the question, like, are you able to deliver on all of the things you just said, given the space constraints?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Yeah, we have been working with our vendors, and we've actually expanded contracts for our current vendors who we have who are open to providing services on the residential halls,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: since that requires less movement and less additional space to provide those services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So we have painting, taping, and spackling that happens on the residential halls.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Many of our young people have actually painted their own halls and their bedrooms after getting that certification.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have had electrical and HVAC provided in the gym and other.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Areas around the facility where our staff is incredibly flexible about ensuring that our young people receive these services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have an art club that in Crossroads that meets both in the residential halls and in the cafeteria.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We'll use any space that we can find to provide those services.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how youth are grouped at Horizon and Crossroads and whether there is a defined policy. Ginsberg describes an admissions interview, court collateral, conflict checks, discussions about where youth feel safe, and facility leadership assessment for safe housing.
chapters.title: Farías asks how youth are grouped at Horizon and Crossroads

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Groups within secure...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Detention.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How are young people being grouped at Horizons and Crossroads?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there a defined policy?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are they divided by age, by charge, by their needs, based on disability or other considerations?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just to get back to the overcrowding,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just wanting to understand how you all make certain decisions on where certain people are placed and how they're placed and what their living conditions are.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So we have a multi-pronged admissions process.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have an admissions team that does an interview with the young people and will look at the collateral information that comes from the courts.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And then our facility staff will meet with the young people to identify which neighborhood they come from.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: If they have any known conflicts in either facility, what their history has been in maybe non-secure detention or in our facilities, and make those decisions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: They will have a conversation with the young person about where they feel safe, and then there is an assessment by the staff and facility leadership about where that young person can be housed safely.

chapters.summary: Farías asks about bathroom and shower availability and about Local 371 budget lines and staff injuries. Ginsberg says there are 40 bathrooms at Horizon and 36 at Crossroads, with 20 youth bathrooms and showers renovated since July 2025; Gendell will follow up on budget and injury data.
chapters.title: Farías asks about bathrooms, showers, and staff vacancies

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So just a question about facilities.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How many bathrooms and showers are available for young people in both the detention centers, respectively?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: There are 40 bathrooms at Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: There are 36 bathrooms at Crossroads.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Since we began a project of expansion in July of 2025, we've renovated 20 youth bathrooms, which includes the showers, and one staff bathroom has been converted for

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: youth use, and another conversion is currently in progress.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And we are exploring creating additional shower and bathroom spaces in both facilities through additional construction.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and just one final question.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What are the budgeted lines and vacancies for the workers, particularly Local 371?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And do you have any data on how many are out due to an injury on the job?

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: In terms of the budget line for the staff, I'm going to have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, and just any data you can provide on the number of staff that are out due to an injury on the job.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: I think we have to get back to you on that one, too.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Folks are missing, so next up, Councilmember Hanif, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer says the issue is not new and asks how the city prevents youth from entering detention and where youth go if they lack stable housing. Ray Toomer describes the Family Assessment Program, borough offices, community-based services, and about 3,000 families served annually.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about prevention and housing stability

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I always have the broader question, which is, if you have, this is not a new issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been around a very long time, so this is not a new issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But the question is, how do you prevent young people in the first place, and those that you do support, which I think you are, if Stephanie's there, I know everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's me talking.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, they're going to go home, but they may not have a home.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do you deal with this bigger issue of prevention in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Maybe looking at the neighborhoods, NYCHA, then they need tons more support in that neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or if they don't have a place, I have 35 foster care kids, it's rough.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But you need someplace to go.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: So we're going to turn it over to Ray Tumor to talk about some of our community-based alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: Thank you, Stephanie.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: And Councilmember Brewer, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: You know, ACS certainly recognizes the importance of both diversion and prevention programs on the front end.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: And so we offer diversion programs for young people after they've already had interaction with the system.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: But we also recognize that it's really important to

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: prevent young people who are at risk of future involvement.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: And so one of the ways we do that is through our family assessment program.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: We have borough offices located in each borough that are staffed by licensed social workers.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: And the family assessment program started as a PINS diversion program, but it is now open to any New York City family who is struggling with the behaviors of their young person.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So they can come into one of our offices, engage with a licensed social worker, and we have a continuum of community-based services that are run by community-based agencies

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: that we contract with to support those families, and we offer an entire continuum of services.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So we have family-based therapies that are evidence-based models, and then we also have youth-specific services that really just kind of follow the youth.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So it really depends on what the circumstances of that family are, but we are dedicated to prevention work,

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: and we serve over 3,000 families per year in those programs, and we have significantly reduced the number of young people who are placed into care on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you think increasing that might help cut the numbers going into Horizon and Crossroads?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're all trying to get the numbers down, and then we're trying to get the young people out of that program, trying to get them back home.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So in terms of our prevention work, it does start really early, right?

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So we're trying to engage young people when they're in middle school who are exhibiting sort of status offenses, right?

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So, you know, skipping school, behavioral issues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have the list?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: of absentee for the middle school and the high schools?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like does DOE give you that list?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Does somebody go visit that family?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Stephanie says no.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: Well, we don't have a specific list of young people, but we do work very closely with the middle schools in our district that tend to send young people into our facilities.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: We do also offer family court alternative to detention programs that do stem the tide.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what would you suggest we need to do to increase those services so that this number and the pictures that...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Councilmember Stevens keeps showing us don't exist.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So I think, you know, the things that were mentioned in the press release is our focus in terms of DOP and Mach J implementing programs in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: I think we've been successful in family court.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: You heard the commissioner's testimony about only six JDs that remain in secure detention, and we want that to even be lower than that.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: But I think we've laid out a plan that clearly identifies, you know, what we think is appropriate for those young people in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, but if you got the list of, because absenteeism is very high at DOE right now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you had that list, would that help?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I would go knock on those.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, DOE is trying to go knock on the doors.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then I'll shut up.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: So I don't think ACS really has, we can't just knock, ACS can't knock on people's doors without authority.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I understand that, but DOE could do that and then you could work together.

utterances.speaker: Stephanie Gendell
utterances.text: Yes, that would be possible, but ACS can't just...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, no, but you could get...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: DOE could say this person needs, it's one administration in case you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: When young people are truant, you know, DOE does make the referrals to our family assessment program and we work directly with that family.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You know how many they make or you don't have that number?

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: DOE is our largest referral source.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So they, you know, like I said, we served over 3,000 families.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: DOE is typically around 40% of those families that, you know, refer 40% of those families to us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ray Toomer
utterances.text: So we do work with them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It sounds like there could be more coordination if DOE would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One administration.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler stresses the crisis and asks about the capacity of new ATI programs and expected population reduction. Popper says Families Rising will add about 20 youth at a time and 40 over a year, while Exalt will expand by 20 youth at a time and she will provide exact totals.
chapters.title: Restler asks about ATI capacity and expected population reduction

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm always near.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really just want to underscore a point that the chair made a few moments ago, which is this is a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I appreciate, Commissioner, you agreeing with that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we really want to see an even more urgent and robust response from the administration in light of the recognition that we have a crisis on our hands.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am, I'm just, I really want to focus, sorry, I don't mean to pause for too long, therefore it was a pregnant pause.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I want to focus on reducing the population and what we can do together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Popper, you referenced a couple of the ATI programs in response to questions from Council Member Nurse that are being rolled out next month.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are you able to speak to the capacity of those programs and the anticipated reduction in the population that we should see from these programs coming online?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Yeah, so the two programs I mentioned earlier, Families Rising, we're going to be increasing their capacity by about 20 at a time, 40 in a year.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: Exalt, which is the one that pairs case management with school support, paid internships, and career pipelines, they are going to be expanding by 20 young people at a time and over the course of a year.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: work with young people for two years post-20 young people at a time to what number total?

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So I can get you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: I believe they were starting around 100.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: So I'll get you the exact number of where they're going to land.

chapters.summary: Restler urges ACS to take population reduction as a mandate and asks how often ACS reviews whether youth can be safely released. Ginsberg describes weekly longest-stay lists sent to youth part judges, engagement with 18B leadership and OCA, and an 8% population reduction since July.
chapters.title: Restler urges ACS population reduction and asks about case reviews

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, I just...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will say one of the most heartening conversations I had earlier this over the course of this first year of the Mondani administration was with Commissioner Richards, who said who was the first DOC commissioner who's ever said to me that he takes population reduction as a as a part of his mandate.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really am looking for ACS to take a similar approach.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not just who gets sent to you and dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's taking the leadership that the conditions are unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We cannot have people sleeping in classrooms, on chairs, that we have to do better, and that we are going to take the lead in driving down this population and holding everyone else accountable and bringing the other agencies to the table.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just trying to kind of understand how often does ACS conduct comprehensive reviews of the current population to determine if youth can be safely released?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: So DC Ginsburg is going to give the detail, but I do just want to just add in here that, yeah,

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: fully agree, urgent, and the importance of collaboration in order to reach that, I'm hoping is what you're hearing from my

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: my panel partners here to work with ACS and then our other partners and community to ultimately be able to work towards that.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: DC Ginsburg can give some of the specific detail to ACS's current actions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have been looking at census since I came through the door.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: As you are aware, I came into the seat from legal aid.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: I spent 30 years at legal aid examining system issues that affected young people, particularly young people who are prosecuted in the adult

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: criminal court system.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We compiled lists every week.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We were sending lists of our longest stay youth to the youth part judges.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We were engaging council.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We were working with the 18B leadership.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: To discuss how young people were being represented.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We were talking about what Ms.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Popper has referenced, and we are extremely, extremely grateful to the administration for looking at expansion for mitigation specialists, for the young people in our custody.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It's one of the most important

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: aspects of representation of teenagers is to create a complete record of the young

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: people's lives up until the time that they came into the courthouse.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And so we are optimistic that having this additional information,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: as the DA referenced earlier, it's important for all parties in the courtroom to know everything about these young people so that cases can be disposed of.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We met with OCA.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The chief judge of New York State and the deputy judge came

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: to the facilities and met with our longest stay young people and heard from them specifically about how the length of stay was affecting their ability to stay engaged in programming, to stay engaged in mental health

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: services, the head of our Bellevue Juvenile Justice,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: mental health services presented to OCA and the chief judges to explain the effects that length of stay had upon the young people's ability to stay engaged.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: OCA facilitated visits of the facility and we facilitated meetings with both our staff and our facility leadership and our young people

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: so that the judges and the court staff could hear from individuals in the facilities about

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: how the length of stay

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: of stay was affecting our ability to deliver services, how it was affecting the quality of life for the young people and the staff, and our ability to deliver services to the young people.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have seen a reduction in population since July of just over 8%.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We are very hopeful that that reduction continues.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Our young people are extremely engaged with us.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Our staff is engaged with us.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We are doing everything that we can to coordinate with both the city, the defense bar, the DA's offices, the

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: OCA to ensure that cases are adjourned more frequently, that the adjournments are shorter, that dispositions happen more quickly where it is possible,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: understanding that some of these cases are extremely complex and need more time, and that adequate services are provided to the cases so that the information that the courts need to resolve these cases is available.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that we have successfully in New York City strengthened public safety and reduced incarceration for decades.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's only during the Adams administration that we saw things move horribly in the wrong direction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I really hope that the most

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: M.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Donnie administration will hold itself accountable to these numbers and that we're going to be monitoring that census every single day and how we can safely drive it down and provide opportunities that are much better alternatives than detention.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about average daily programming hours and reports that youth spend hours with nothing to do. Ginsberg explains the split school schedule, GED and college classes, after-school programs, and vocational and arts programming, and says ACS provided about 10,000 hours of programming last year.
chapters.title: Restler asks about daily programming hours for detained youth

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to ask one more question, if I may, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm just concerned that, you know, and I really do want to thank and recognize Local 371 and the workers who are trying in really challenging conditions to support the young people and keep everybody safe.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really want to thank all of the workers in Horizons and Crossroads for that work and for the union for their strong leadership.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am concerned that as a result of the lack of community facility space, the kids are spending hours and hours every day with nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I'm wondering if you could share the average number of hours per day that youth are participating in programming.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're getting reports of kids only participating in programming on a weekly basis and that there's a lot of sitting around.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And just wondering if there's updated data that you can share with us on kind of average hours per day in programming.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So I'll start answering that question with explaining how we've arranged school.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Because before we had this age population in the facilities, there was just a regular school day from 8.30 to 2.30.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Now, because we have a larger number of students who are participating in GED, all those kids used to go to school together.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So if you were in high school and you were getting your GED, everyone sat in class together.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have worked very closely with New York City Public Schools to separate out that

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: that schedule.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So high school runs from 8.30 to 2.30, GED runs from 3 to 6, and the college classes run

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: intermittently during the week depending on what time the professor is available and when we have space.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: When we have individuals in school, in high school, we may be running workforce development on the halls.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So there may be young people doing HVAC on their halls or painting on their halls while the

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: other the younger kids might be in high school.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have a full after-school program that DYCD funds, and those services are held by, we contract with CCA, and CCA subcontracts for

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: those services, and we have a broad array of services that come in as an after-school program.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And we've seen many of our young people are engaged in culinary and barbering and music programming.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have a new DJ program that's extremely popular with our young people.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have restorative justice.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have a new program that we have contracted with Inside Circle that

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: came to New York City from California through Project Restore, and they are now in the facilities running restorative circles with our young people.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We have a relationship with Brownsville Cooking Collective that is teaching cooking classes.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: We're running a six-week pilot.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate you providing this list.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have data?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Yes, I do have Dana.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yes, and could you, if while you're looking for that, we're going to move on because we need to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez and then Councilmember Nurse has one question.

chapters.summary: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez asks about the gap in mental health care after youth are released. Ginsberg says successful access is not a high number, many youth are excluded due to behavioral histories or charges, and ACS is working with Bellevue and H&H while noting mental health is not directly an ACS function.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about post-release mental health care gap

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So I have two main questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: One is around the mental health.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As you know, when we met on Friday at Crossroads, I was really taken aback by the level of challenge it is for a young person post-release to seek these mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It seems like, obviously,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: for a lot of them, this is the first time they're engaging with a mental health expert when they're in these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So yes, I'm aware of the challenges, but what role does ACS play in staying in contact with these young people once they're released?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can we be more aggressive to fill in that gap?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just refuse to accept that

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: you know, for the population that is released, they're kind of left on their own to researching and calling.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then as you all shared on Friday, for whatever reasons, a lot of these providers just don't have the capacity, just don't want to take on these youth for whatever reasons.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like we should be stepping in, we should be providing, we should be figuring out how to provide these services directly to these youth once they're released.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So what is, is there another plan?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there additional investments?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How are you all?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: responding to this gap.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So the mental health question, the mental health- Can you bring your mic in?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The mental health services continued service issue is a very real issue.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And it is being pursued both by our partners at Bellevue, Juvenile Justice, Mental Health Service, H&H is looking at it.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The administration is very aware of it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And they are all- Do you have a sense of how many, I'm sorry to interrupt, I just have limited time.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of when they are released, do you have a sense of how many of them are successfully accessing care versus how many are not?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It is not a high number.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It is not?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It is not a high number.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Many of our young people are excluded because of their behavioral histories, because of their pending charges or their prior charges.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It's a crisis in the city.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I get it.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So we work in partnership with Bellevue, Juvenile Justice Mental Health Services.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: And there are folks in the administration looking at solutions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, I will follow up.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how many youth currently in detention will be released before age 21. Ginsberg and Gaston say release decisions are made by courts and are not knowable in advance by ACS.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks how many youth will be released before 21

utterances.text: My next question is, of the current population, can you share how many will be released before they turn 21?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have that data?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: That is up to the courts.

utterances.text: That's not a decision that we can make.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But you don't have, it's not information that you have.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: It's not information that's knowable.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, you're not aware?

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Their release is dependent on a court action and decision, and so we don't have a way of...

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Knowing what the court action or decision is going to be in general.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks about gynecological care and whether any detained youth are pregnant. Ginsberg says there are seven young women, they receive trauma-informed medical care including gynecological care, and no pregnancies are known; basic care is in-facility and advanced care outside.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about gynecological care and pregnant youth

utterances.text: And my last question is for the females in detention.

utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So we have seven young women right now.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: They receive regular medical, and that includes gynecological care.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: All of our care is trauma-informed.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: If they need additional care,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: care they receive that they're taken outside of the facility for that we do not have any pregnant young women that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay and the gynecological care is that at the sites or is that one of the examples where they're taken outside?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Basic care is done in the facility and more advanced care is done outside the facility.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is gynecological considered advanced?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm just saying if you don't know, how do you expect these young women to know to ask?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: Well, our medical, H&H provides our medical care, and they know, and we can get back to you in as much detail as you want as to how they handle that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just, I would, I mean, we very briefly spoke with them, and I just want, like, I just think it's important for them to be surrounded with this information, whether or not it's, like, readily available, but, like.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think it's important for them to know, like, if I'm requesting, if I want to see a gynecologist, I might have to be taken out of this facility versus not.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: I think what I will just add to the fact that we've got health partners that we're working with is we have case managers that are working with our young people on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: And so there's a few avenues for which young people can raise particular concerns.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: addition to talking to the medical person in particular.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Nurse asks how many staff have case review for early release as part of their explicit job duties. Ginsberg says executive staff review cases; Popper says juvenile case information is legally limited and OCA/judges review, while Gaston says ACS is working on a data agreement with MOCJ and state partners.
chapters.title: Nurse asks who reviews detention cases for early release

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I think that's what he was looking for.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: My question is, and this is the same issue we had with correction in terms of case review, is how many people, like how many staff members

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: actively look like it's in their job description to look at the cases of the individuals that are in detention.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: So it's really at this point me and my executive staff that are looking at it.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Ginsberg
utterances.text: The staff in the facilities really don't get involved day to day.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So that's how many people.

utterances.text: I'm just trying to get down to the nitty gritty because we had to like really hammer down into the nitty gritty to get more capacity for case review to advocate for you all to have more staffing.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: So, and can you repeat exactly?

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So, and just because I know the chair is going to pop off on me.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: How many people have in their job description or as an explicit ask that they are supposed to be reviewing cases of people in juvenile detention for

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: We're working very closely with the Office of Court Administration, and they are making sure that the cases in secure detention are being reviewed by judges and the court stakeholders very regularly.

utterances.speaker: Miriam Popper
utterances.text: And that is one of the reasons why we are meeting so often with them is to talk about what are we doing with long-term cases.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So do you all, so nobody who works in these facilities is able to say, these 20 young people, we highly recommend that they get released early.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Like, we are advocating for them with OCA or whoever is the ultimate decider.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rebecca Jones Gaston
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I just think like we don't need, you know, we've never needed legislation to do any of this stuff.

chapters.summary: Stevens returns to her crisis question and recalls the March 2020 COVID-era effort when courts, defenders, prosecutors, and agencies quickly identified youth who could go home safely. She asks why that model is not being used now; Popper confirms the 2020 effort occurred.
chapters.title: Stevens presses on crisis response and COVID-19 precedent

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have questions here.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I have questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I want to go back to my first question when I asked, were we in a crisis?

utterances.text: Are we in a crisis?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I am asking everyone here, why are we not doing that right now?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So again, like these are things where I'm like, we have a formula.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We did something that was needed to be done because we're in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Right now, it's a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So we need to look at that work and get it done.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And like not sit here and say like we have this thing that's that I know it's supposed to have 150 it still hasn't gotten online so that's not a sense of urgency
