utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I need to know who authorized a water gun fight where young people are using water guns and taking pictures and throwing up gang signs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have pictures of that as well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm telling you, as I'm sitting here, people are texting me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is serious.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I need to know who authorized this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sergeant Roms, you can take this to them as well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: These are the pictures that were sent to me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm telling you, the amount of people that have been coming into my office, I'm just like, we should all be at the table.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, we got to figure this out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We got to figure this out right now.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I need to know who authorized this water gun fight and then tell the young people that they shouldn't be out in the streets using guns.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, that to me is some psychological stuff that's going on.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I can send this all to you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm literally sitting here and people are sending this to me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: My staff was sent all of this stuff today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: These are serious things.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is not just about overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so this is being exasperated because it is overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we also have to take accountability for what is actually happening right now.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm really unclear about who authorized that and why was this okay and how is this happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I've been in youth development for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I would not sit here and tell young people that you shouldn't be doing something and then authorize a water gun fight to the young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And in my testimony, we talked about 96% of those kids in there are black and brown young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that's a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I see Councilmember Joseph is back.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have a lot more questions, so you can ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They didn't ask any of them.

chapters.summary: Council Member Rita Joseph says this is the fourth hearing on these facilities and that numbers, conditions, and outcomes remain the same. She says a plan must be executed, cites the eight-hour riot, and urges the administration to move the system.
chapters.title: Joseph criticizes repeated hearings and lack of progress

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, so we will circle back so you can answer some of those questions as to who would, that's careless behavior to even authorize that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm just going to say something before I even start with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The level of frustration is because this is the fourth hearing we've had about this.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: These two institutions when it comes to young people.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I did it when I was the chair of education, when no schools were happening for these young people.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I had a joint hearing with Councilmember Stevens on the conditions inside.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We did it on the MDRs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We did it on the IEPs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We've done and done and done.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The numbers remain the same.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The conditions remain the same.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And the outcomes are not as great as we would expect them to be.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If you put out a plan, you have to execute the plan.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We cannot let the plan just sit there and say, we have a plan.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But why isn't the plan working?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I think tonight, as a team, you probably have to go and sit around the table and figure this out for you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: young people.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This is the level of frustration for us.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Every time I go there, it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We're reading the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You have a riot for eight hours that you cannot control?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: These are young people.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This is unacceptable on every level for us as moms, legislators, and folks who drive policy in this place.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And these are young people that look like my four boys.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I hope you guys get it right.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Commission, I know you weren't here, but we hope you can put on some roller skates and start putting some work into this and really move this system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Absolutely committed to both looking into the concerns that were just raised by Chair Stevens, but also this is a priority and has been my focus, frankly, since I've been here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And working with our partners again across the administration, our community partners, and in partnership with you at the council, absolutely

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: look forward to being able to come back and share the improvements and the successes and the advances.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about the timeline for temporary classroom units being developed by ACS, DDC, and SCA. Administration witnesses say they are waiting for final state approval and hope the classrooms are ready in the next couple of weeks; construction renovations at Horizon and Crossroads are underway with completion around 2027.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about temporary classrooms and construction timelines

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When we were there, we noticed that construction of temporary class units.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What is the timeline for completion of the ACS, DCC, and SCA development and installation of temporary classrooms that will create additional space for educational programming?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We worked really closely with the School Construction Authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Got that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we're hoping they're actually in place and ready to utilize.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're just waiting for the final approval from our state partners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we're hoping in the next couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And you will alert the committee once it comes online?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are there construction plans for renovation of Horizon Crossroad or both?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Because that's one of the other things that we talked about, the conditions where the young people are.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You have to update and renovate those spaces for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're asking about the...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Renovation and updating infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There is renovation happening at Horizon with an anticipated completion date the end of 2027.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the renovations at Crossroads, a similar timeline.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When are you starting and it's ending in 2027?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The construction has already begun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're in different stages at both facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And what we have been able to do with the support of our

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: fellow agencies across the administration is actually get construction expedited so that they are usable spaces far more quickly than originally planned and anticipated by almost two years.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about trailer capacity, staffing, and whether the trailers will be used for non-school programming. Administration witnesses say each trailer holds 16 students, ACS staffing ratio is one to six, the focus is classroom space, and other uses will be explored with state oversight.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about trailer capacity, staffing, and programming use

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What's the maximum capacity of each trailer?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many young people can safely use the space at one time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's 32, 16 in each trailer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and just to be clear, for the classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the classroom spaces.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It will be inspected, ready for young people, and staffing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And staffing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: For the young people when they go into those trailers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: For the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What is the ratio per student?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The ratio related to the education folks is in the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Our staffing ratios for our staff with the young people is one to six.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: One and what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, one to six.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: One to six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Which is different than the Department of Education's requirements.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Beyond their intended use for school-related activities, will young people be able to use the trailers for other programming, such as after-school programming, tutoring, mentors, arts, sports, youth development initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Because I know you're creating it because you lack space, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What else will you be doing in that space once you create it?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Nothing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we don't necessarily have a plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Part of that will be in conversation with our state oversight to make sure that we can do different activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And our focus has been really on classroom space currently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then once we have young people,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: people in those classrooms getting their education, we will happily be exploring with our state partners what approvals we can get for the other utilization.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I do want to be clear that they are not going to be utilized for sleeping spaces.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Oh, that's good to know.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks who will manage the trailers and whether classes get suspended when staff are insufficient. Administration witnesses say ACS will manage, staffing ratios are met with specialized uniform positions escorting youth, and classes are not suspended facility-wide, though individual classrooms may pause.
chapters.title: Joseph asks who manages trailers and whether classes are suspended

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Will ACS or DOE be responsible for managing this trailer, coordinating programs, ensuring young people have access to the space?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's ACS.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: ACS will be managing them?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you have enough staff to escort young people to class?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And if you don't, do the classes get canceled?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the staffing ratios, we currently have coverage for the staffing ratios.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are continually, as was stated earlier, kind of in a constant hiring phase to make sure that we're continuing to bring on additional staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we have met the staffing ratios as required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And DC Ginsburg can add to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we've created specialized uniform positions to support school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so those individuals ensure they go to the halls in the morning, they escort the young people to the classrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have ensured that we have adequate staff to move the young people to school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When do you decide reasons for suspending class?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Who decides that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is that ACS, DOE?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Who decides if class gets suspended?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We generally do not suspend classes if there's a particular incident that happens where we have to remove young people from a classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We might do that for one particular classroom, but that will not affect the entire facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's not our practice to suspend class.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You've never had to suspend classes before because of an incident?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And if you have, how many times?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I do, we certainly have had to remove young people from a particular classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have not,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: stop school in the facility, facility-wide, in maybe two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It was probably two and a half, maybe three years ago.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about the Exalt expansion and reentry coordination with New York City Public Schools. Popper says Exalt added $400,000 for 20 slots per year, DOE court liaisons are returning, and transition coaches are planned; Joseph raises a student who took two years to return to school and describes a continuum-of-care gap.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about Exalt expansion and school reentry

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In September, you announced Promise Expand Education Employment Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What specifically is new and what is the budget and when does it start?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That was part of the announcement.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That was MopJ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so that was an alternative to incarceration and detention program that we were expanding called Exalt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that program we added an additional $400,000 to to cover an additional 20 slots per year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's a program that pairs young people with very intensive case management as they're getting out of detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Make sure that they have support in their educational needs, and most importantly, connecting them with paid internships and career pipeline assistance.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And those who have to return to school, how do you work with New York City Public Schools for reentry?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What does that look like?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so we're actually bringing back our Department of Education court liaisons to make sure that they're in every court so that individuals who have court cases going,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the court has the information they need to understand where they are in their school process and the attorneys can work with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The attorneys and the families can work with Department of Education as well to navigate the, you know, does there need to be a safety transfer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Does there need to be a different school that they're going back to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then we're working closely with the Department of Education as well on transition coaches for that transition back from detention as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I always talk about this one student that was caught up in the system.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Took them two years to get back to school.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You have a young person who was brought up on gun charges, who is a D75 student.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It took them two years for New York City Public School.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Where's the continuum of care when they leave your system?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Where's the continuum of care?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: There's a big black hole.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Y'all just drop the kids, and there's no continuation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And then they get caught up again, and we're like, oh, my God, they're back.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But there was never any support when they left your system to support them in carry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, and we're certainly in conversation with the Department of Education about that, and most importantly, bringing transitional care inside the facilities, so we're increasing our investment in transitional care inside,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: so that every young person has a warm handoff, and that includes with the Department of Education, and making sure that there is someone who knows their educational situation when they are inside, what they want to see happen next,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and where they want to be headed educationally when they get out so that they can be coordinating with the Department of Education before they leave the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that can be teed up for them.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How long does it take for you to connect with their home school that they came from if they are returning back to that school?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can follow up with our providers and see how long they need to connect with DOE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But that's also a relationship we're working on building.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether ACS tracks attendance and graduation outcomes after youth leave detention. Administration witnesses say that is a New York City Public Schools function and that student data is protected.
chapters.title: Joseph asks if ACS tracks outcomes after release

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: ACS, do you track attendance on graduation outcome?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you track the youth when they leave you?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And what data can you share with the council when they leave you?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What data do you have?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are you tracking the students when they leave the system?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's a New York City Public Schools function.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So you guys don't talk to each other?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Their data is protected.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about class suspensions and staffing for moving youth to school. Administration witnesses say classes are not stopped facility-wide, though individual classes may be paused, and ACS has specialized uniform staff to escort youth to classrooms.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about class suspensions and school-movement staffing

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I just have a point of clarity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So you guys, so it was, I know Councilman Joseph just asked about classes being suspended or canceled, and it's your understanding that that doesn't happen or that does happen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It has not happened facility-wide.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So it happens on an individual basis?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It may happen that a particular class needs to be stopped for a particular time on a day, on a particular day.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How often is that happening?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Not that often.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I'm, again, in real time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm getting texts from your staff saying that classes are often canceled or suspended and then packets are handed out on the hall to the young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I was in a real time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And they also wanted me to say that they don't have adequate staffing ratios with the movement of young people across to classes.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about the city's plan for state Raise the Age funding, including $194.5 million earmarked for ACS. Administration witnesses say the FY26 plan was submitted and is awaiting state approval, and the FY27 plan will follow once FY26 is resolved.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about state Raise the Age funding plan status

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have some funding questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In fiscal 2027 preliminary budget, $300 million of the baseline state funding was added to the sweep.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Sweep for city funds in fiscal 2026 and in the outer years across several agencies including 194.5 million specifically earmarked for ACS.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The city is

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: required to submit a plan for this funding that was subject to OCF's approval.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has ACS submitted this plan for expenses for fiscal 2026, fiscal 2027?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has it been approved?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If not, when does ACS expect to submit the plan?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is there an anticipated timeline for approval?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's two plans, one for fiscal year 26 and one for fiscal year 27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The fiscal year 26 plan has been submitted to the state and we are awaiting approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Once we have approval on the 26 plan, we'll be able to put together the 27 plan, knowing how it gets resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I just want to, while we have the moment, say we are really grateful to the state for that $300 million.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'll be more grateful when they fully fundraise the age, so I'm not grateful.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What is included in the city's plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I don't actually, we don't know yet because it's still awaiting approval from the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But for the fiscal year 26 plan, since we're now in 27, it's for things that have already been funded.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is the funding being used to support the administration plan to reduce the overcrowding?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is any of that money being used for that part of the plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the fiscal year 27 plan, which is the year we're currently in, is still in development, so I don't have the answer to that now, and the people are still working on the plan, so it's not like I'm not sharing it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Do we have an idea of, like, what's taking so long?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I just, I know that we're, we focused on the 26 plan and getting that approved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And while we're working on putting together a plan for 2017.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And it's still not approved from 26.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And like, we're currently in the fiscal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks for funding details for each program in the administration's announcement, including units of appropriation and budget codes. Administration witnesses give amounts for Families Rising, Exalt, Fortune Society, and Center for Community Alternatives, and say contracts will be backdated to October 1 and appear in the November plan.
chapters.title: Stevens asks for funding details on ATI expansions

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The administration announces new investments, including expanding alternative to detention incarceration plan and non-secure.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you outline the funding for each program mentioned in this press release and each agency's budget, including units of appropriation and budget codes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as we've talked about before, the Families Rising program is one of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's an additional $344,000 that's being put into that, taking that budget from approximately $1.6 million to $2 million for the Families Rising program.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The budget code for that is 6020.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Then the EXALT program, sorry, was there another question beyond budget code or?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Including unit appropriation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Unit appropriation for that one is 006.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the EXALT program has an additional $412,000 per year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's taking it from approximately $1.1 million to $1.5 million.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Unit of appropriation, again, 006 and budget code 6020.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have also included in that investment that was announced, Fortune Society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: which has an additional roughly $800,000 that was added to its budget for in-custody transitional programming as well as in-community reentry programming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the unit and the budget code remain the same for both of those, for both Fortune and then the Center for Community Alternatives, which had an additional $618,000 added to it,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that all will be backdated in their contracts to October 1st.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When were those resources added to the budget and will we see adjustments related to the announcement in the November plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, according to OMB, they will be in the November plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They are added to Mach J's budget as the contracts are registered.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether the administration has a long-term goal to expand community alternatives and reduce secure detention funding. Administration witnesses say they are assessing whether courts and youth use the programs, because programs only reduce population if court stakeholders rely on them.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about long-term funding shift to alternatives

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Does the administration have a long-term goal to expand funding for those programs and reduce funding spent on secure detention?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If not, why?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We absolutely are, as we are implementing these, we are needing to assess how they are being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Are they being used, are these the programs that the youth in our community actually need, and are these the programs that our court stakeholders are going to use?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we know that we can make as many programs as we want, but if the court stakeholders don't rely on them, then they won't be used and they won't be effective in our goal of reducing population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as we are implementing them, we are meeting with the stakeholders all of the time to see if these programs are meeting their needs, and then we move to the next thing and figure out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is there more investment needed here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is there more investment needed somewhere else?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether Close to Home is part of the plan and about non-secure detention capacity. Administration witnesses say Close to Home is for post-disposition family court placements, not detention, and that non-secure detention has 87 beds with 50 youth and nine more coming online.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about Close to Home and non-secure detention

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is close to home part of the administration's plan to reduce overcrowding and detention?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If so, how many close to home slots are currently available and filled, and are there plans to expand the model?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'm going to take that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are not permitted to use close to home for detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Close to home is for young people who have been through the family court who are placed by the family court post-disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I think what you're getting at is do we have an alternative where we could place young people besides secure detention, which we've been using non-secure detention as a discussion and

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: that's also in the release as an item that we're pursuing currently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so I do have information about non-secure detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you'd like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we currently contract with five providers for seven non-secure detention sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We currently have 87 beds and 50 youth in them, and we are in the process of bringing online an additional nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so we believe we'll be able to have enough capacity in non-secure for the young people in detention who, as part of the work we're doing, the court is willing to step them down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They'd have to be juvenile offenders to step down into NSD or to get originally placed in NSD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: rather than secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I do have the budget code if you're looking for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do we need the budget code?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The contracted budget is $18.4 million.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The unit of appropriation is 008.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The budget code is 2350.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The object code is 640.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I honestly don't know what any of that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that funding includes the nine beds that are not currently online but will be soon.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks how ACS designates youth as travelers and what sleeping arrangements they have. Administration witnesses say 109 youth lack bedrooms, 74 are on residential halls, and a smaller number cannot safely be housed on halls due to conflicts; ACS assesses daily whether youth can move to halls.
chapters.title: Stevens asks how ACS designates travelers and sleeping arrangements

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: During our visit at Horizon, staff explained that young people who are held above the certified capacity are referred to as travelers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Travelers are not assigned to a bed or a room or to keep their belongings.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Do you not receive the same level of educational instruction or tutoring as other residents, and they sleep in repurposed classrooms and makeshift beds?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How does ACS determine which young people are designated as travelers?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is the designation based on intake date, security certification, or other criteria?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How long does a young person typically remain as a traveler?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'd like to provide some clarification as to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have 109 young people today that do not have bedrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 74 of those young people are on halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it is our goal to put every young person who can live with other young people on our residential halls into those residential halls

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: because it allows them to program with those young people, go to school with those young people, and allows for a larger group experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a smaller number of people, young people, who cannot safely be housed on the halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so they are placed in alternative housing classrooms or other rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Every day we are looking at those young people because we are a detention facility and young people are released and enter every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we assess whether or not there is a hall composition that has changed to allow a young person who perhaps could not live on a residential hall

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the day before, they may be able to live on a hall the following day or the following week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are making those assessments so that we have as few young people off of residential halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: as possible.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But how is that determined?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So with all of that, I'm still confused on like, how do you determine if you like other, like you said, some of them have security issues, but what if they don't have security?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, how is that determined?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You said it's a small number.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How are you determining that small number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Most of them have, almost all of them have security issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So they have either had conflict in the community with the young people who are on the halls, or they have had conflict in the facility with the young people on the halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes we will try to move them from one facility to another to ameliorate those issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's not always possible.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether youth without bedrooms can securely store personal belongings. Administration witnesses say there are no youth locker rooms, but each youth without a bedroom has a bin for private belongings.
chapters.title: Stevens asks whether travelers can secure belongings

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Do young people or do the travelers, aka young people, have access to secure locker space such as locker rooms or are they able to secure their personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we don't have locker rooms other than for staff in the facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Each young person who does not have a bedroom has a bin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That they can hold their private belongings.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about steps to prevent and find contraband. Administration witnesses describe TSA-level scanners, x-ray machines, handheld x-ray scanners, tools to open fixtures, announced and unannounced searches, wands, metal detectors, and pat frisks, with contraband logged and held by ACS police.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about contraband prevention and searches

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Preventing contraband, what are some specific steps have staff at Horizon and Crossroad taken to identify and reduce contraband that is brought into the facility?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we have done a number of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As you know, because you have come into both of our facilities, we have TSA level scanners at the front entry and at the sally port for young people who are going to appointments

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: outside of, including court and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have x-ray scanners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have acquired handheld x-ray scanners that can look through opaque surfaces such as mattresses or walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have acquired additional

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: tools that can open light fixtures and radiators and soap dispensers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Anything that can be opened, we have acquired tools to open it to identify whether or not anything is being hidden in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have recently, because the new legislation has been passed on the state,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have recently procured x-ray machines that we will be able to use once the state issues regulations and we're able to formulate policy for the use of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We anticipate use of those machines in early 2027.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have some questions about the x-ray, but I have some more questions about the contra.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How often are searches done in the facility and what type of searches are conducted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there's a variety of searches that are done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When staff come on a tour, they're supposed to do room searches on the halls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When young people move to the school, they are wanded with a trans frisker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They sit on a boss chair and they walk through a metal detector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A pat frisk may be done at any time when young people are moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And after court and after searches and after visits, additional searches are done of the young people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Are searches announced or unannounced on the housing areas?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I'm hearing that searches are typically done on Tuesdays, and most of the young people know when it's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They are both announced and unannounced and can happen on any day.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Who's in charge of making such searches and conducts them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: leadership sets the, provides the authorization as set forth in our policy.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you ever conducted staff from refraining from conducting searches without your authorization?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What's the protocol and chain of, what's the protocol when contraband is found and confiscated?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have a policy that controls contraband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's generally, if it is, so both our uniformed staff and our ACS police conduct searches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They often conduct searches together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They will...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They will put that contraband into bags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They will make sure that it is logged, and then it is held by the ACS police.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: One of the things that I'm hearing and getting intel from is that contraband was collected on Hall H at Horizon on June 21st.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you tell me a little bit about what contraband was found from Hall H?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There were some sharp objects that the young people turned over and at least one blade.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about x-ray body scanners that use iodine radiation and whether ACS plans to use them. Administration witnesses say ACS is not using them or storing them on site, and is waiting for state guidance and DOHMH guidelines on who would be scanned and how often.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about x-ray body scanners and radiation concerns

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I want to ask questions about the x-ray body scanners.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The state passed legislation authorizing the use of x-ray body scanners to screen for contraband and juvenile detentions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Those scanners use iodine radiation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Advocates, including legal aid societies, have raised concerns that staff levels of radiation exposure for minors are not well established and that the scanners frequently produce false positives.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Has ACS installed or begin using body scanners at Crossroads or Horizon?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If not, does ACS plan to?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And what is the timeline?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are not using them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do not have them on site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are waiting for guidance from the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have been in discussions with New York City DOHMH who set the guidelines for New York City DOC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At the point they set those guidelines, the 16 and 17 year olds were on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we are waiting to see what the state

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: guidelines are, we don't know what they are yet.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If ACS plans to use the scanners, who would be scanned and how often would a single young person be scanned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are waiting for the guidance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The guidance will control that.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks what security changes were made before the June 21 Horizon violence and whether earlier warnings were flagged. Administration witnesses say they would need to review history and provide information later, and describe scanners, training, staffing, and commissioner town halls with staff.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about pre-June 21 security and staff protocols

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Prior to violence at Horizon on June 21st, several issues have been reported to ACS, including instances of assault on staff and attempted by young people to obtain keys.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How significant security or optional adjustments were made to prior to 21st incident?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you speak to early reports that had flagged concerns concerning security issues at Horizon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I can't speak to, we would have to go through the history to provide that information to you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, I would like that to be provided because that's one of the things that I'm concerned about, like, because according to staff, because like I said, they're coming and incoming, they're saying that they had been

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: really highlighting that this was an issue and these concerns weren't taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: According to the fiscal year 2026 mayor management report,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: rate of youth on staff assaults and altercations were with injuries and detention fell to 0.21% to 1.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The tensions fell from 0.21% to 0.13%, indicating per 100 youth in the average daily population.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Social services employees, union, SEU, local 371, which represented many staff, has called for a review of safety protocol.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What specific steps has ACS taken in the past year to improve safety at Crossroads and Horizon?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What additional measures are planned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So part of what is in place and in plan are the scanners and the hand wands and the examples that were provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think the other pieces that we're doing is continuing to look for ways in which we are able to...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Both provide training to staff around safety protocols for themselves, the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: conflict resolution efforts, and the additional

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: staff that we are hiring both from the youth development specialists and that line, but also our special officers just continuing to add

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: ways in which we are able to both do planned and unplanned scans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The other piece for me that was really important was making sure to actually meet with staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I've had the pleasure of having several town hall listening sessions to hear directly from the staff around what their concerns are, what are the things that they want me to keep top of mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that has been really critical to my thinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: and the conversation around what are the things that we need to be putting in place and the safety of our staff is just so critical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Their ability to do their jobs, and it's a really, really, really, really hard job, is

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: top of mind for me and continuing to find ways that we are able to support them across the board is really critical and continuing to hear about what ideas actually staff have about solutions is actually also critical.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I was very happy to hear that you, that's one of the first things you did was come in and like meet with staff, but I am sure today, as soon as we're done, we have a whole

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: list of people ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm sure you will hear additional things and concerns that they have because again, like I said, since that press conference, I have been bombarded with the amount of young people talking about how they feel young people aren't safe, the staff not feeling safe.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Again, I just got a picture of piles and piles of garbage that are outside of Hall A, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And just trying to understand, like, and I'll send this to you as well, outside of Hall A at Crossroads, there's piles and piles of trash.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How is that acceptable for young people to, like, have that?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How are we even addressing that?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm really concerned.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm sure today we're going to hear from a number of folks.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: From local 371 to really kind of like speak to

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: some of that.

chapters.summary: Stevens notes five former youth development specialists pleaded guilty to accepting bribes and smuggling contraband. She asks what ACS has done since 2024 and how many staff were disciplined; administration witnesses say they will follow up with data and describe screening and bag policies.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about staff contraband and disciplinary data

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: On October 24, four, I mean five former youth development specialists at Crossroad pled guilty to charges of accepting more than $50,000 in cash bribes to smuggling marijuana, razor blades, prescription pills, and other contraband into the facility.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Since 2024, what steps have ACS taken to prevent staff from bringing in contraband into facilities?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Specifically, what changes has ACS made to staff screenings at entering, background checks, supervision, internal monitoring, and how many staff members

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: have been disciplined or referred to investigation for contraband-related incidents since 2024?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we will have to get the specific data for you and follow up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What I will say is, you know, a big piece of safety and security in the facility is trying to prevent contraband from coming in as well as

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: confiscating it and finding it if it is already in the facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the scanning, all of those measures are things that staff have to actually go through as they are entering the building and there are requirements according to policy around

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: what type of bag or not, can you bring in, all of those sort of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we will happily follow up with the specific data that you're asking for.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks whether frontline facility staff participate in the justice working groups. Administration witnesses say they are not sure but will check and appreciate the suggestion.
chapters.title: Stevens asks whether facility staff join justice working groups

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I have a question too, because I know that you've done some town halls, but as these working justice working groups are coming together, do we have a working group that actual staff who work in the facilities that are part of to be able to have their concerns addressed as well?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I know that we have like a reduction population, this, this, that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But how do we get feedback from the people who actually work in the facilities?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not actually sure, but we can definitely check and appreciate the suggestion if it doesn't exist.

chapters.summary: Stevens says attorneys report they cannot bring laptops into Crossroads and Horizon and have had video-visit problems. Administration witnesses say attorneys can bring laptops with clearance, and that video-system issues were resolved with case-manager support.
chapters.title: Stevens raises attorney laptop and video visit issues

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Attorneys representing young people in the detention have told counselors that they are not allowed to bring laptops into Crossroads and Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If so, what is the policy?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And why was this adopted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They can bring in their laptops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They just need to get clearance.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So are they not getting clearance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They should be getting clearance.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I had a number of attorneys who reached out to me who said that they have not been able to bring in their laptops and they feel like this is not fair representation and they have serious issues.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In addition to when they are trying to do even the...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I guess FaceTime video conversations because you've changed, I guess, providers multiple times that they've been having trouble with that as well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think when we changed systems, there were some attorneys who had trouble adjusting to the new system, but we had case managers who were available to walk them through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And those issues have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, I don't think those should have been issues because we have to, you know, fair representation is really important.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So hopefully that won't happen again.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks about MOCJ's ATI program guide, noting only five programs accept youth ages 13 to 15 and only one Brooklyn program is borough-based. MOCJ witnesses say they track referrals and are aware of the need for more local and mobile programs because travel and safety affect attendance.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about Mach J ATI access by borough and age

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have some general questions for Mach J.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: According to Mach J's 2026 ATI program guides, only five ATI programs accepted young people between the ages of 13 to 15, and only one program in Brooklyn is Brooklyn borough-based.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As a result, young people in Queens and Staten Island who need site-based programming may have to travel to other boroughs, which can and makes it hard to attend consistently, particularly for young teenagers who have a long commute after school.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Does the Mach J track whether distance or lack of local program affects referral enrollment and completion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We certainly track all of the young people coming into our programs and where they're based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are aware of the fact that there needs to be more local programs and programs that are mobile and can go out to the young people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do have programs available for every borough, but we are aware that there are sometimes safety issues getting to the programs and having more mobile programs that can come to them is crucial.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Yeah, I...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know that's one of the big things that D.A.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Clark and when I spoke to the DS at Nylund, this is a huge issue that kids are not getting on the boat to come to these programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so really thinking about are we making it accessible?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks what options exist for youth excluded from ATI programs due to disabilities or serious mental health and substance use needs. MOCJ witnesses say programs do not exclude charges, but if mental health is the primary issue they want treatment first; Stevens says there are not enough programs and the gap must be closed.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about ATI exclusions for mental health needs

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Many youth ATI programs exclude young people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: serious mental health or substance use needs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Others have change-based, have other exclusions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What options exist for young people who don't qualify for any programs?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Does MACJ track how many young people are turned away and why?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I want to clarify a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The programs are not necessarily excluding individuals with mental health issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All of our programs do have individuals who struggle with mental health challenges in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's more about whether a mental health issue is the primary issue, and that needs to be dealt with before they can start working on school, before they can start working on internships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If it's the primary issue, we want to make sure there's a program that is addressing that first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that is something that we are working on with Department of Health, with the State Office of Mental Health, on making sure that those programs to address mental health as a significant need are in place.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we already know that that's already a problem because we are, when the kids are leaving the detention, we don't have places to refer them because folks are at capacity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So that sounds like it's a circle there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And part of what we're working on with this Youth Justice Working Group is the circle, is the continuum of the programming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so in our prevention group, one of our biggest focuses is community-based mental health and having mental health services available when the youth are growing up to their family and not just when they get.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to the justice system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that's the most important piece is not having these programs be justice system programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Oh, I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm all about prevention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we're in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so we have to walk and chew gum at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So while we're thinking about prevention, because I'm clear, kids should not be getting services and mental health services for the first time in secure detention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let's be clear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean that's not what's happening currently.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so if you're saying that you have programs that exclude kids because their first primary issue is mental health, and then we're saying that we can't refer them out because there's no programs that are accepting them, then what do we do with these kids?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like right now, not preventative because we already didn't prevent it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We already failed them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So now what happens?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So these young people are being referred to the programs that currently do exist by the programs they're with, and we're making sure that we are expanding access to those programs and ensuring that they do not have charges.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: In the rollout, was those programs that you expanded, are those the programs that allow access to young people with the mental health services?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The programs have no charge exclusions at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If somebody, again, if their primary issue is a mental health issue.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: These young people who have primary mental health issues don't have programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That is the correct answer because it's no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are not enough programs for them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what are the programs currently for the young people with mental health issues that that's their primary focus?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's what you just said.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What are the programs?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: programs that they can be referred to right now, today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So they can be referred to DOHMH programs in the community of federal qualified health centers?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's interesting because when we were at the facility talking to the mental health worker, he said that a lot of times they're not accepting the kids because they're at capacity and because they have

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: they have charges that they aren't accepting them into those programs.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what other programs other than H&H that are saying that they're not taking those kids to?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, so we're working closely with Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So the answer, again, is we do not have programs that are addressing young people whose primary issue is mental health.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The answer is no, and it's okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If we're going to sit here and go around in circles to say, just say no, so that we can say no, we've got to figure this out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We need to figure out what that program is.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let's get a program and, like, figure it out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's no.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And if we sit here and say, like, well, we could do this and that, it then gives us a gap to think that there's something there that it's not.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You don't have to answer it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'll do it for you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We do not have programs for young people who have mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, I'm not doing this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because I want us to now say, if that is a gap, let's figure out how to close this gap.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Full stop.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks when MOCJ will release the new ATI RFP. Administration witnesses say new programs will come online at the end of FY28 and the procurement will be released a few months before FY29 begins.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about Mach J ATI RFP timeline

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Mock J extended its ATI contracts for one year while it's developing new procurement.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When will the new RFP be released?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The new RFP will be released, the new programs are going to be coming online at the end of FY28, and the new procurement will be released a few months before the start of FY29.

chapters.summary: Stevens dismisses the administration panel, saying she has many more questions but does not want to hold public witnesses. She thanks them, says the conversation will continue, and states that young people deserve better.
chapters.title: Stevens dismisses administration panel and thanks them

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have so many questions still.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: However, I have so many people here who are signed up to testify, and I do not want to hold them hostage any longer.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So at this time, I'm going to...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Dismiss this panel.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I want to thank you for the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And also, this is not the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is a work in progress.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And again, my frustration is that these young people deserve better.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I will fight to the end to ensure that they get it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And the sense of urgency needs to be for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Everyone should be fired up and pissed off that these kids are not getting what they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And since no one else is, I will do it all on my own.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because this is not okay for me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I do not pretend and sit here and pretend like I don't.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I like this is not political for me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is my life work.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: These young people deserve better and we are failing them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: All those young people that are in secure detention, each adult in this room needs to look at it as a failure on their own.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I take that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: as serious that we're failing kids.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so we need a sense of urgency.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I will continue these conversations because I have maybe like 30 more questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'll be sending them over looking for responses.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens calls a five-minute break before public testimony. The hearing pauses and resumes later.
chapters.title: Stevens calls five-minute break before public testimony

chapters.summary: Stevens opens the floor to public testimony and reminds attendees this is a formal proceeding requiring decorum. She explains the witness table rules, appearance cards, three-minute speaking limit, and how to submit written testimony.
chapters.title: Stevens opens public testimony and explains rules

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm now open the floor to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Before I begin, I would like to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but they may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you wish to speak today, at today's hearing, please...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait for your name to be called.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Once you are recognized, you have three minutes to speak about the oversight top of New York City's secure detention conditions and youth incarceration policies.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or written testimony you may wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: To testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Please note that audio and recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: When you hear your name, please come to the witness panel for the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: For the first panel, we will be calling Anthony Wells, DeColby Hester, Derek Robinson, and Cassandra Washington.

chapters.summary: Anthony Wells, president of Social Services and Employment Local 371, testifies about unsafe juvenile facilities. He says the union has no faith in local management and reminds the committee that these are secure facilities, not group homes or summer camps.
chapters.title: Local 371 President Anthony Wells testifies on unsafe facilities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: Ready?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: First of all, thank you, Chair and other council people for calling us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: I want to thank the ACS Commissioner who is still in the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: I want to thank her for doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: My name is Anthony Wallace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: I'm the President of Social Services and Employment Local 371.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We represent several titles in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: juvenile facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: The most prominent one is the YDS, Youth Development Specialist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: I am going to be very brief because I want you to hear from these folks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: It's ironic that I started my city career at Sparford Juvenile Center as a caseworker many, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: Let me say this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We have been trying to work with the agency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: with this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We have no faith in the local management of the facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We don't believe they are honest with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We don't believe that they share information with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
utterances.text: We don't think they even recognize us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Wells
