utterances.text: We emphasize, though, that the council must also ensure that money received by the state for RTA-related expenses is invested in community-based programs that connect young people with support and care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: As for Intro 447, this bill reflects the plain truth that raise the age can only succeed if courts and attorneys are aware of the full scope of community-based options that are available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: When attorneys, judges, and other stakeholders operate under outdated or incorrect information about existing programs, it may lead them to overlook these options and needlessly order detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: Intro 447 will ensure that courts and attorneys are better educated and better equipped to meet young people with care, not incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: But distributing resources is, of course, not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: ACS and the City Council must also continuously engage judges and attorneys on community-based programming and connect them with providers so that they fully understand the landscape of services offered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: With regard to Intro 629, we do worry that it will have harmful unintended consequences and may otherwise be unworkable as written.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: We do not agree that ACS is the appropriate agency to house the review teams proposed by the bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: We are alarmed that while participation on review teams is mandatory for some stakeholders, ACS would only have to make reasonable efforts to include public defenders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: Contrary, these panels should not be allowed to function unless there is representation from advocates whose sole motivation is the interest of the young person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: Further, as written, the panel is meant to collect and review information that would presumably require the cooperation of the young person, which should only take place with the knowledge and advice of counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: And lastly, if I may, given the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: Range of psychosocial information that panels are supposed to consider, we believe that more guardrails should be established to ensure the utmost confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: The aim of this bill is, of course, worthwhile, but the potential for unintended harm is too significant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Moss
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens tells the panel that Councilmember Restler is open to amending Intro 629 and urges stakeholders to reach out. She thanks the panel and notes David Moss is no longer with LDF.
chapters.title: Stevens says Restler open to amending Intro 629

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, you'll be happy to know Councilmember Ressler is very open to amending his bill, which was

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: part of our negotiation for us to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I know that a lot of folks did reach out to me and Councilman Ressler around some of the issues that folks have with the bill.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so he is very open to amending.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So please reach out to him so that those things can be heard and considered and get this bill to a place.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because again, like I will repeat, we're in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And wait, you're not with LDF anymore, huh?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm like, wait.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Look at that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm like, wait, David, you're not over there anymore.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I do not have any more questions for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you guys so much.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We'll be going to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: For the next panel, we will be calling Jason Rodriguez, Wendy Calderon-Payne, Jackie Gustigian, Jacqueline Goodman, and Veronica Leventhal.

chapters.summary: Jackie Gazdigian of Brooklyn Defender Services says incarceration harms youth and increases recidivism. She reports youth still sleeping on floors, benches, and common areas, supports Intro 447 and Reso 274, and calls for the Youth Justice Innovation Fund and Youth Justice and Opportunities Act.
chapters.title: Jackie Gazdigian testifies on detention harm and alternatives

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: My name is Jackie Gazdigian.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: I'm Senior Supervising Policy Counsel at Brooklyn Defender Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: I want to thank the committee, Children and Youth, and Chair Stevens for the opportunity to address the council about youth incarceration policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: And also thank you so much, Chair, for visiting Horizon a few weeks ago and viewing the conditions in person and speaking with the children who were there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: Incarceration, even in short stays in detention, is extraordinarily harmful for young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: Research indicates that placing youth in locked detention centers pending their court dates leads to worse public safety and youth development outcomes and higher rates of recidivism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: This is because incarceration causes substantial long-term harm, including decreasing a young person's ability to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: In order to decrease the population of incarcerated youth and break the cycle of re-arrest, it is imperative that we focus on alternatives to detention and keep young people in the community with their families, while providing them the supportive services they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: We commend the Council and the Mayor for their commitment to significantly reducing the number of youth who are incarcerated in detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: These facilities are still extremely overcrowded, and the young people we represent, who we just spoke with their social workers, report sleeping on the floor in classrooms still, on benches and intake, and other common areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: And given ACS's continued staffing and management challenges, the potential for harm in facilities must be front of mind as we focus on our efforts to minimize young people's entry into detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: We are pleased to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: that program spots at Families Rising and Exalt have been increased and there will be more opportunities for alternative to detention programming for ICM, which is intensive community monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: If more spots for community-based ATD programming come online, more kids can be released from secure detention pretrial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: But the truth is that the longer a young person is detained pre-trial, the more likely that their case will be resolved with a sentence of incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: And this is one of the reasons we support Intro 447, which will require the city to publish a guide on available diversion programs for young people facing detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: Additionally, we support Resolution 274 and urge the Council to pass a resolution in support of the Youth Justice Innovation Fund, which would direct $50 million

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: of raise the age funding to community-based organizations to provide a continuum of services for youth age 12 through 25.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: And I'll wrap up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: Lastly, one of the biggest drivers of youth incarceration is mandatory minimum sentencing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: And we all heard already from the DA's office in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: We asked the council to support and pass a resolution urging the enactment of the Youth Justice and Opportunities Act, which would expand opportunities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: for programs and other alternatives to incarceration and immediate record sealing for young people up to age 25 and give judges, not prosecutors, the discretion to decide what kids can get a program instead of going to jail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jackie Gazdigian
utterances.text: We are grateful to the City Council for holding this important hearing today, and we look forward to continuing to work with the Council to reduce the number of youth who are incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Jason Rodriguez of the Legal Action Center shares that he was incarcerated for 24 years beginning at age 18. He describes fear and hypervigilance in detention, supports Intro 447 and Reso 274, and says programs must have capacity and accountability so detention is a last resort.
chapters.title: Jason Rodriguez shares lived experience and supports alternatives

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: Good evening, Chair Stevens and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: My name is Jason Rodriguez, Policy Associate at Legal Action Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: I am also formerly incarcerated, having spent 24 years in prison, beginning at the tender age of 18.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: When I read about the horrid conditions young people at Horizons and Crossroads, I think about my time spent on Rikers and similar conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: I could have a book open and still be listening for trouble instead of taking the words in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: I hid fear and vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: When I needed help understanding what I was actually feeling, protecting myself came before learning or imagining a future beyond any of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: These conditions are an urgent threat to young people's health and development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: They shouldn't have their days worrying about safety instead of learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: A safe place to sleep and consistent access to school and care cannot wait until overcrowding is resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: The city must work with defense attorneys, courts, and community organizations to identify what's keeping young people detained and use community-based alternatives to the fullest extent possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: With support tailored to each young person, detention should always be the last resort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: Legal Action Center supports Intro 447 because accurate information can help more young people be considered for alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: But a program list is a guide must be also able to accept them and meet their needs and conditions without what other providers with additional care is needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: When space or services are lacking, the city must find them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: and help them proceed with those people so they can have more possible alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: We also support Resolution 274, which calls for state legislators and the governor to give New York City access to raise the age funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: Community-based alternatives must be a priority for those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: Giving supports and those options, allowing providers to reach those young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: The city must demand accountability and reforms, especially given the reports in September.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: And I will just conclude with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: We cannot keep asking young people to change while having them live in conditions that we are responsible for changing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Rodriguez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Veronica Leventhal of the Center for Family Representation describes a client in secure detention who cannot meet with his therapist due to lack of private space and staff. She says he primarily speaks Spanish but lacks Spanish-speaking instructors, asks for community funding instead of detention, and supports Reso 274.
chapters.title: Veronica Leventhal describes client denied mental health care in detention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: My name is Veronica Levin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: My name is Veronica Leventhal, and I'm the Deputy Director of Social Work in the Youth Defense Practice at the Center for Family Representation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: It's been a really long day, so I'm going to get straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: I've worked with kids who have been arrested for almost 10 years, and kids get arrested because of environmental factors, because of systemic poverty and racism, because of difficulties in school, and because of insufficient mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: And those things are only exacerbated and worsened when they are in detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: So what we are asking for you today is to consider funding programs and services that help kids outside of detention rather than funding detention itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: I have a client right now who's housed in secure detention and he is sleeping in a hall where it was formerly some other space that's been transformed into bedrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: And because there is a lack of private space on that hall, he cannot meet with his therapist there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: And he cannot be brought down to the mental health office because of a lack of staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: So he just isn't getting sufficient mental health care while there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: He also primarily speaks Spanish, and there are, at this point in time, he says there are no instructors in the school who speak Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: So instead, they give him packets to work on, but sometimes those packets are also in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: And I understand that that is a DOE issue, but I think it should be mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: We appreciate the intent behind the bills before the committee today, but we believe that more concrete measures are necessary to meaningfully improve the conditions within detention and reduce youth incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: We believe that a stipend should be offered to families of children returning home from incarceration to ensure to help them, to help kids who need to go to programming and appointments and court dates, to set them up for success and reduce recidivism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: I also want to point out I've heard many people speak on the need for more mitigation specialists in the youth part, and I know people who have applied to that panel who have not heard back for more than six months to be approved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: And the help is out there if we can just eliminate the bureaucratic nonsense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: Ideally, the raise the age law should also be altered so that adolescent offenders can go to non-secure detention instead of secure detention, alleviating some of these space concerns.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: We urge the council to pass Resolution 274 in support of the Youth Innovation Fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Veronica Leventhal
utterances.text: We also urge the council's support in passing both the Youth Justice and Opportunities Act and right to remain silent, and we thank you for the opportunity to be heard here.

chapters.summary: Jacqueline Goodman of the Legal Aid Society describes inhumane conditions at Crossroads, including youth sleeping in classrooms and hallways and some forced to use trash bins due to lack of bathroom access. She notes state agencies declined to renew overcrowding waivers and calls for decarceration and returning a significant number of youth by December.
chapters.title: Jacqueline Goodman describes inhumane conditions at Crossroads

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair and members of the City Council, although Chair, I see you're the only one here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Thanks for sticking with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: My name is Jacqueline Goodman and I'm an attorney with the Legal Aid Society and I was actually visiting clients at Crossroads on Friday when you and fellow council members were there and I appreciate you making that visit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: We are glad to see the Mamdani administration begin to take action to address the crisis that is the inhumane, overcrowded conditions young people have been subjected to for several years at Crossroads and Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: These conditions are the foreseeable consequences of a system that incarcerates far too many young people,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: forcing many to sleep in classrooms and hallways, deprived of an adequate education, appropriate programming, and, unbelievably, leaving some with no choice but to urinate or defecate in trash bins due to a lack of bathroom access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: These unsafe and unacceptable living conditions demand an immediate fix.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Even OCFS has finally declined to reissue a waiver of state regulations that purported to greenlight the city's overpopulation of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: And it appears that the State Commission on Correction is declining to do so as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Every day, these children in the city's care are being harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Although the new administration has taken some steps to address this crisis, sustained and urgent action remains necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: We must decarbonize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: This requires ensuring that there are adequate and appropriate opportunities for alternatives to incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: The city has 50 new beds underway, but this is unlikely to suffice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: The city must invest in young people before they become system involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: In year-round paid employment, community-based programs,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: credible messengers, and safe spaces where young people can learn, grow, and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: We call on the administration to work to safely return a significant number of young people, as you, Chair Stevens, have also called for,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: to their communities by December, and to demand accountability from the NYPD, district attorneys, and judges whose decisions contribute to this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Our children deserve safety, dignity, education, and opportunity, not overcrowded facilities that fail to meet their most basic needs and cause them affirmative harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacqueline Goodman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rev. Wendy Calderón-Payne of Bronx Connect proposes expanding Functional Family Therapy in schools and a Philadelphia-style pre-diversion program for first arrests. She says length of stay is unacceptable and that ATI capacity exists but placement requires DA approval and excludes some serious charges.
chapters.title: Wendy Calderón-Payne proposes prevention and ATI expansion

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Chair Stevens and members of the committee, I'd like to thank you for allowing me to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: I am Reverend Wendy Calderon-Payne, and I'm the executive director of Bronx Connect, and I know everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: I have submitted written testimony, but I feel that I'm going to use my three minutes to answer some questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: In terms of reducing populations of horizons and crossroads, first you must work to prevent youth getting involved in the justice system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: New York City funds an excellent family-centered mental health program called Functional Family Therapy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: If this was expanded, it could be offered to schools with high levels of violent incidents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Data shows that many of these incidents revolve around a very few number of students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: The crisis management system includes a school-based gun violence prevention program that could be expanded to the same schools to work in conjunction with the FFT program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: We have a Philadelphia pre-diversion program for youth facing their first arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: This program is in partnership with the Philadelphia DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: This incredible program allows us to enroll a young person upon their first arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: When they graduate, the arrest is not registered anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: This program has maintained a 6% re-arrest rate for over five years, and I do not know of this happening in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: As a city, we should want youth facing their first arrest to be diverted, and a pre-diversion program would allow us to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Their life trajectory and not have it

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: have a justice record, follow them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: I have proposed launching such a program through city council for the last few years, and I'd love to have further discussions with you about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Second, the length of stay must be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: It is just unacceptable that young people are detained for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: The reason we have so many older young people in Horizons and Crossroads is because their cases are not being addressed by the courts in an expedient fashion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: It is not a speedy trial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Finally, I encourage the committee to review the charges these

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: these detained youth and young adults are facing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: As a program that does work within Horizons, many of these young adults are facing serious charges like murder, attempted murder, gang jumping, and are facing decades of incarceration upstate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Few judges and DAs will allow an alternative to incarceration program for youth facing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: rape and murder charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: That's just the truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: While 95% of Bronx Connect's felony cases are high felonies, less than 1% are rape or murder charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Finally, I think the quickest way to move, the quickest way to reduce the population is to move people from secure detention

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: and into community alternatives, of course the DA has to approve this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: It's not our choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: It's not ACS's choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: We would take everyone, but they have to be approved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: I'd also like to clarify that our ATA program has significant therapeutic services and bilingual services, but we cannot

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: to an ATI program, anyone who needs to be in a mental health facility, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: The DA won't allow it, but we have a lot of bilingual therapists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Stevens asks Calderón-Payne about DA approval for ATI placements and capacity. Calderón-Payne explains that a legal aid attorney can refer a youth, but the DA must accept the program or allow non-secure detention, and felony limits restrict eligibility; Stevens says she will review youth for possible placements.
chapters.title: Stevens questions Wendy Calderón-Payne on DA approval for ATI

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I just wanted to let you know something that you said around the capacity of programs, and I was telling my committee counsel

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: that that's something we should definitely be looking at as we are thinking about this legislation to make sure that we're not just having a list that's not updated, but we should have the capacity and ongoing so that people know that if it's full or if it's almost at capacity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So that's definitely something we're going to add to the bill because that's something that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And Reverend Wendy, yes, you know how to find me.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I have actually lots of questions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But the one question I'm going to ask you, because I know you just said the DA has to approve for the young people to come there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So, like, the DA has to offer it, or is this?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: So we can have a legal aid attorney come to us and say, I have a young person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: But in the end, it has to be the DA has to tell the judge they're accepting of the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: And in terms of the young people who are in Horizons, the DA has to say, yes, I will move this to like a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: I'll move the charge and allow them to have non-secured detention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: So if it's a juvenile offender charge, they had to have been under 18 when the first arrest happened, and it had to have been only one felony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: But I really think you should look at how many felonies are people facing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Because if it's two or three, they can't get that non-secured attention.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I think that's even why the DA Clark was saying that she doesn't even know the young people that's in there to be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I will offer them to review to see if there's young people in there that have that and that can be moved into your program.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And do you have capacity currently?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: Of course, every ATI, I can say this across the city, has capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: But again, so, and we take high felonies, let the record state, we take high felonies, we take gun charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: But the 200 people we have interacted with in the last two years, only three cases have been, it was one rape and two murder charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: And I think one of the murder charges might have been like a self-defense against an abusive boyfriend of a mother, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: But we don't get those charges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: The city does not fund an intensive program where a judge or a DA will give those charges to a community alternative.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I mean, thank you to this panel.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'll be in touch to continue to have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Calderón-Payne
utterances.text: You have my number.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know where to find you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You're down the block from my office.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you, guys.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you for this next panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We will be calling Daniel Alva-Willatron, David Freudenthal, and Raymond Lyles.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And in addition, if your name has not been called yet, but you intend to speak, please raise your hand and fill out an appearance card with Sergeant at Arms.

chapters.summary: Youth advocate Daniel Alva-Willatron with Youth Represent calls for rebuilding the system and investing in youth programs. He says youth need direction, paid employment, stipends, culturally competent mental health care, and credible messengers, and names programs like Exalt, Youth Justice Network, CASES, and Exodus.
chapters.title: Daniel Alva-Willatron calls for rebuilding system and youth investment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: All right, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: My name is Daniel Abawoletron.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I'm a youth advocate with Youth Represent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I'm an artist and a believer that the system that we have now needs to be completely broken down and rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I would like to thank Chairwoman Stevens and the members of the committee for giving me a chance to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I would like to start off with the fact that gangs were formed to protect black communities, but as we know now, times have changed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Young people need direction and support to understand that they have the power, that they can have power in a positive way and embody their self-worth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: The city will keep sending youth to detention if we don't invest in these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: These programs that do this work, programs such as Exalt, Youth Justice Network, Cases and Exodus, and many others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: A lot of these programs use preventative measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: and enforce self-empowerment, as I definitely know y'all heard about preventative measures earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: These programs provide youth with credible messengers, aka mentors, who can help youth get into even more programs and stay out of trouble.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: They have the experience and can come to young people and say, this is who I was and this is who I am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: They can aid youth in changing from who they are now to who they can become.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: When young people are given the right resources and opportunities, it's unbelievable how far we can go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Young people need money, paid employment, stipends, even access to funding and grants for young people to build their own programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: We need education about advocacy skills, other programs that are available, networking outlets, and maintaining those outlets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: We need mental health treatment and therapists or psychiatrists who can understand cultural competency and meet young people where we're at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: This means options to work with gender expansive therapists as well as therapists and psychiatrists who are from the same racial background or have similar lived experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: People with the most relevant lived experiences sometimes can't even get licensed as a social worker, therapist, doctor, and etc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Because of background checks and restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Youth doctors and counselors should be proactive in their work and we should feel like the people around us actually care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: And those people should also be reaching out to us if we miss appointments to try to figure out what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: If you don't have the youth in the forefront, change is never going to come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Youth want to be heard, but too often we get shut out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: We get painted in a negative connotation, but we have a voice and every

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: Everyone should just let us be our voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: That was pretty much that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: So I thank you all for your time today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: See, it's just me.

chapters.summary: Stevens thanks Alva-Willatron for bringing the youth voice and apologizes that he waited. She says young people should speak first in the Children and Youth committee, and he says he does not mind waiting and will testify again.
chapters.title: Stevens thanks youth advocate and says youth should speak first

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Well, thank you for coming in and being the youth voice.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I should have let us know you were here because I always let the young people speak first.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So next time, make sure you just let them know that you're a young person and you get to skip the line because.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Children and youth is about the young people, and your voice is just as important, if not the most important in the room.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I apologize that you actually waited and had to wait because I believe you guys should be first.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So next time, just write youth on there, and we'll make sure you get to the top of the line.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I have no problem waiting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: I've testified many times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniel Alva-Willatron
utterances.text: You will see me next month, too.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This is the youth committee.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Youths go first.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I don't think anybody objects to that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I just want to.

chapters.summary: Council staff asks whether anyone in the chamber still wishes to speak and then calls remaining Zoom registrants. No additional speakers raise hands.
chapters.title: Council staff calls remaining public speakers and Zoom registrants

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If there is anyone in the chamber who wishes to speak but has not yet had the opportunity to do so, please raise your hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Seeing no hands, we will be making a call for Zoom registrants who have not yet spoken.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you are currently on Zoom and wish to speak but have not yet had the opportunity to do so, please use the raise hand function and our staff will unmute you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We are calling Jason Rodriguez, Luis Alfonso Martinez Rojas, and Vanessa Persaud.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So we'll give another opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Use the raise hand function.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We don't see anyone.

chapters.summary: Stevens closes public testimony, thanks community members, the ACS commissioner, DA staff, and attendees who stayed all day. She reiterates that the city is in a crisis, calls for urgency, thanks council members and officials, repeats the goal of getting 150 youth out by December, and adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Stevens closes public testimony and adjourns hearing

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Seeing no hands, I would like to take note that everyone can submit written testimony to testimonies at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I would like to extend my thanks and dedication to the community members who offered their testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Could we give a special shout out to our ACS commissioner who is still in the room listening to the testimony?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Could we give it up for her?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And oh, you're not supposed to clap in here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm such a bad habit.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But yes, special shout out to her.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Special shout out to all these people who stayed the entire time, who was here since 12.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Also, we have the DA staff who's also still here.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I want to point this out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's like usually by the end of my hearings, it's usually me and my staff.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But this is an important topic.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I want to reiterate, we are in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I need everyone to be moving at the expeditious rate as if it is a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so we want to continue to work together, work as a community, because, again, every young person that is in secure detention is a failure on us as adults in this community.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you, everyone, for showing up.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you to all the council members who showed up because my committee is a tiny one because my committee is a tiny one.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But we had all these council members show up and a public advocate and the borough president to say that this is an important issue and they want to be heard and we want to work together and get this done and get 150 kids out of secure detention by December.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And with that, this hearing is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: The Committee on Children and Youth held an oversight hearing on secure detention conditions and youth incarceration policies, with testimony from the Bronx DA, ACS, MOCJ, Probation, unions, advocates, families, and youth.

Major themes included overcrowding at Horizon and Crossroads, youth sleeping in common areas or classrooms, staffing shortages, violence and contraband, long pretrial stays, and barriers to alternatives to detention.

The committee also considered Intro 447 on an alternatives guide, Intro 629 on youth detention review teams, Intro 977 on training about sexually exploited youth, and Reso 274 on raising the age funding for New York City.
title: Committee on Children and Youth
topic: Oversight - Secure Detention Conditions and Youth Incarceration Policies in New York City
